papers.title: Ternary Feature Masks: zero-forgetting for task-incremental learning
papers.authors: Marc Masana, Tinne Tuytelaars, Joost van de Weijer
papers.mechanism: For each new task the network grows by N new features (units/channels) per layer. Ternary masks on activations mark each feature, per task, as unused, forward-only (frozen) or trainable. New features read the frozen old features, but old tasks' masks exclude the new ones. Per-task normalisation parameters and per-task heads make forgetting zero by construction (0.0 measured).
papers.overlap: Gives the same guarantee as NSA: new-task features are invisible to old tasks, and new heads read old plus new features, exactly and without stored data. The difference is how invisibility is achieved: here by new coordinates plus task-conditioned masks (width grows each task and the forward pass depends on the task), not by an additive write projected into old heads' null space inside one fixed-width shared vector. NSA is essentially a basis-free, fixed-width version of this.
papers.setting: supervised vision (fine-grained datasets, ImageNet); task-incremental (task ID at test time)

papers.title: Progressive Neural Networks
papers.authors: Andrei A. Rusu, Neil C. Rabinowitz, Guillaume Desjardins, Hubert Soyer, James Kirkpatrick, Koray Kavukcuoglu, Razvan Pascanu, Raia Hadsell
papers.mechanism: Each new task adds a full new network column. Earlier columns are frozen. The new column receives lateral connections, through small nonlinear 'adapters', from the hidden layers of every earlier column. Each task has its own output layer reading its own column.
papers.overlap: Already has: frozen old modules, exact retention at every state with no stored data, the new skill reading old features, and later skills reusing all earlier features (the skill-chain property). Missing: the single shared fixed-width vector, the null-space projection and the head-copy initialisation. Width and parameters grow per task, and lateral parameters grow quadratically.
papers.setting: deep RL (A3C; Atari, 3D Labyrinth); task-incremental

papers.title: Side-Tuning: A Baseline for Network Adaptation via Additive Side Networks
papers.authors: Jeffrey O. Zhang, Alexander Sax, Amir Zamir, Leonidas Guibas, Jitendra Malik
papers.mechanism: A frozen base network B and a small trainable side network S are combined additively, R(x)=alpha*B(x)+(1-alpha)*S(x), and a task-specific readout reads R. In incremental learning each new task gets its own side network and decoder. The base and earlier side networks are frozen, so earlier tasks cannot be forgotten.
papers.overlap: For one new skill this is NSA without the projection: additive side features on a frozen trunk, read by a new head, with the old head untouched. There is no vector shared across tasks (each task's representation feeds only its own decoder), later tasks do not reuse earlier side networks, and there is no null-space constraint.
papers.setting: supervised vision incremental learning (iCIFAR, iTaskonomy) plus other adaptation settings; task-incremental

papers.title: Self-Composing Policies for Scalable Continual Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Mikel Malagón, Josu Ceberio, Jose A. Lozano
papers.mechanism: Each new task adds a module and freezes all previous modules. The new module uses output and input attention heads to query the frozen modules' action-space outputs, then adds a correction from its own internal policy. It can therefore reuse one previous policy, compose several, or learn from scratch. Parameters grow linearly with the number of tasks.
papers.overlap: Already has, in continual RL including the Continual World Meta-World sequence (CW20): exact retention by freezing, one module per task, and later tasks reusing earlier tasks' knowledge. Composition works on previous policies' action outputs, not on features added into a shared hidden vector, and there is no null-space projection. It is the natural continual-RL baseline for NSA skill chains.
papers.setting: continual RL (SAC on Meta-World CW20; PPO on ALE SpaceInvaders/Freeway); task-incremental

papers.title: Sim-to-Real Robot Learning from Pixels with Progressive Nets
papers.authors: Andrei A. Rusu, Matej Večerík, Thomas Rothörl, Nicolas Heess, Razvan Pascanu, Raia Hadsell
papers.mechanism: Applies progressive networks to robot RL. A column trained in simulation is frozen, and a new column for the real robot (or a new task) reads it through lateral connections. Training is deep RL from pixels with sparse rewards on a Jaco arm.
papers.overlap: Already shows the freeze-and-add recipe for adding a manipulation skill to an RL policy: exact retention of the source policy and fast transfer from the frozen column, faster than fine-tuning. No shared vector and no null-space projection.
papers.setting: robot RL (A3C), sim-to-real manipulation; sequential tasks/domains

papers.title: TAIL: Task-specific Adapters for Imitation Learning with Large Pretrained Models
papers.authors: Zuxin Liu, Jesse Zhang, Kavosh Asadi, Yao Liu, Ding Zhao, Shoham Sabach, Rasool Fakoor
papers.mechanism: A large pretrained visuomotor policy (frozen CLIP encoders plus a GPT-2 temporal decoder) is adapted to each new task or task suite with a small adapter set. The paper compares LoRA, bottleneck adapters, prefix tuning and RoboAdapter. Only the adapter, the FiLM fusion and the policy head are trained; old adapters are stored and swapped back in for old tasks. LoRA with about 1% trainable parameters gave the best post-adaptation performance on LIBERO, with zero backward forgetting.
papers.overlap: Makes the same empirical claim as your one-pair result: a frozen trunk plus a small adapter learns the new task about as well as full fine-tuning, with no forgetting. Adapters are task-conditioned (one active per task) rather than summed into a vector read by all heads. A new adapter is initialised from the previous one, but adapters are never composed.
papers.setting: imitation learning, robot manipulation (LIBERO); task-incremental

papers.title: Memory-Efficient Policy Libraries with Low-Rank Adaptation in Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Samuel Valland Lyngset, Tor Viljen Raanaas, Gard Sveipe, Eirik Møller Nilsen, Jim Torresen, Kai Olav Ellefsen, Tobias Lømo
papers.mechanism: A pick-place base policy trained with PPO on Meta-World (Sawyer) is kept frozen. LoRA adapters are then trained with PPO for other tasks (drawer-open, hammer, window-open, etc.) to build a library of specialists. Success rates show no significant difference from full fine-tuning, with 20-160x less memory.
papers.overlap: The closest match to your current evidence: PPO, a pick-style expert as the base, a frozen base plus one low-rank adapter per skill, and new-skill success on par with full fine-tuning. It does not measure retention, compose skills or share a representation across heads, and has no null-space idea. Unreviewed preprint.
papers.setting: RL (PPO), simulated manipulation (Meta-World); per-task specialists, task ID known

papers.title: Continual Learning in Low-rank Orthogonal Subspaces
papers.authors: Arslan Chaudhry, Naeemullah Khan, Puneet K. Dokania, Philip H. S. Torr
papers.mechanism: Each task gets a fixed low-rank projection P_t, mutually orthogonal across tasks, applied to the final feature vector before the output. The whole network keeps training with weights constrained to be orthonormal (Stiefel manifold, Cayley retraction), so task gradients stay near-orthogonal through depth. A tiny replay buffer is used on the harder benchmarks.
papers.overlap: The closest precedent for splitting one shared last-layer vector into orthogonal per-task subspaces, each of rank about m/T, much like NSA's 8 of 256 dims per skill. But the shared network is retrained, the projection selects what each head reads rather than where new features are written, and forgetting is small but nonzero. No frozen trunk and no additive adapters.
papers.setting: supervised vision (Permuted/Rotated MNIST, Split CIFAR, Split miniImageNet); task-incremental, multi-head

papers.title: Progressive Prompts: Continual Learning for Language Models
papers.authors: Anastasia Razdaibiedina, Yuning Mao, Rui Hou, Madian Khabsa, Mike Lewis, Amjad Almahairi
papers.mechanism: The base language model stays frozen. For each task a new soft prompt is learned and concatenated with all earlier, frozen prompts. Task k runs with prompts 1..k, so later tasks reuse earlier task-specific parameters while earlier tasks keep their own shorter prefix.
papers.overlap: This is the 'each task reads its own prefix' design: exact retention plus forward transfer from earlier modules, with no projection at all. It is the unprojected alternative a reviewer will set against NSA (head j reads h0+g1+...+gj). Prompt space, LLMs, no RL.
papers.setting: LLM (T5, BERT) text classification; task-incremental

papers.title: Learning multiple visual domains with residual adapters
papers.authors: Sylvestre-Alvise Rebuffi, Hakan Bilen, Andrea Vedaldi
papers.mechanism: Small domain-specific residual adapter modules (with BN and a classifier) are inserted into a shared ResNet. The shared, domain-agnostic filters are pretrained and then frozen, and only the adapters are trained for each new domain. The paper notes this 'preserves the original task exactly', like a tower model, without adding new feature channels per domain.
papers.overlap: Already has per-task additive residual modules on a frozen backbone with exact retention. It explicitly contrasts itself with channel-adding 'tower' models, which mirrors NSA's fixed-width versus PNN's growing width. But each domain runs with only its own adapters active (a task-conditioned forward pass), adapters do not compose across domains, and there is no projection.
papers.setting: supervised multi-domain vision (Visual Decathlon); domain ID known

papers.title: Organizing recurrent network dynamics by task-computation to enable continual learning
papers.authors: Lea Duncker, Laura N. Driscoll, Krishna V. Shenoy, Maneesh Sahani, David Sussillo
papers.mechanism: A continual-learning rule for RNNs that projects each weight-update gradient on both sides. The input side is projected away from the span of previous tasks' input activity and the output side away from previous tasks' output activity, using regularised activity-covariance projectors (a Kronecker-structured projection). New-task dynamics are pushed into orthogonal, output-null subspaces.
papers.overlap: The ML precedent for the 'output-null space' idea, and the same family as your earlier Kronecker-block projection that failed in closed loop. It constrains weight updates using activity data, so it is approximate. It adds no modules and does not use the exact algebraic null space of frozen linear heads.
papers.setting: supervised RNNs on neuroscience cognitive tasks; sequential, task-cued

papers.title: Order parameters and phase transitions of continual learning in deep neural networks
papers.authors: Haozhe Shan, Qianyi Li, Haim Sompolinsky
papers.mechanism: A statistical-mechanics theory of continual learning in deep networks, comparing one shared readout with task-specific readouts (multi-head). In the multi-head case, representation changes that stay in the null space of task 1's readout leave task 1's output unchanged (zero forgetting). Forgetting appears once changes leave that null space. The paper also identifies 'catastrophic anterograde interference'.
papers.overlap: Analyses NSA's key fact, that old heads cannot see changes in their readout null space. It is an analysis, not a method: no adapters, no explicit projection, no RL. Cite it for the principle.
papers.setting: theory/analysis (supervised); single-head vs multi-head task-incremental

papers.title: CLARE: Continual Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models via Autonomous Adapter Routing and Expansion
papers.authors: Ralf Römer, Yi Zhang, Yuming Li, Angela P. Schoellig
papers.venue_year: IEEE RA-L 2026 (accepted, per arXiv comments); arXiv 2601.09512
papers.mechanism: Bottleneck adapters are added as parallel residual branches, M(x)=M_pre(x)+A(x), on selected modules of a frozen flow-matching DiT policy (the observation projections and AdaLN). A layer is expanded only when layer-wise feature-novelty z-scores exceed a threshold. At test time, autoencoder discriminators pick one adapter per layer, with no task ID. The base and earlier adapters stay frozen.
papers.overlap: A recent robot example of additive adapters on a frozen policy writing into a shared stream. Protection comes from routing (only the selected adapter is active), not from a null-space constraint. So retention is measured rather than guaranteed (near-zero negative backward transfer) and depends on routing and feature drift. RSS reviewers are likely to cite it as current robot continual-learning work.
papers.setting: imitation learning / VLA (LIBERO plus real Franka FR3); task-agnostic, no task ID

papers.title: InfLoRA: Interference-Free Low-Rank Adaptation for Continual Learning
papers.authors: Yan-Shuo Liang, Wu-Jun Li
papers.mechanism: Each task adds a LoRA branch, W += A_t B_t. The down-projection B_t is fixed before training: its rows lie in the new task's input subspace and in the orthogonal complement of old tasks' gradient/input subspace, which DualGPM maintains. Only A_t is trained, and branches are merged into the weights after each task.
papers.overlap: A per-task adapter constrained not to interfere with old tasks, but on the input side, using stored subspaces of old inputs, so it is approximate. This is the GPM-style protection you found fails in closed loop, and it blocks learning when the new skill lives in the old skill's subspace. NSA's constraint is output-side, exact and data-free; draw that contrast.
papers.setting: supervised vision with a pretrained ViT; class-incremental and domain-incremental

papers.title: PackNet: Adding Multiple Tasks to a Single Network by Iterative Pruning
papers.authors: Arun Mallya, Svetlana Lazebnik
papers.mechanism: After each task, low-magnitude weights are pruned and the network is briefly retrained. The surviving weights are frozen for that task, and the freed weights are used for the next task. At test time a per-task binary mask selects that task's weights, so earlier tasks are preserved exactly given the task ID.
papers.overlap: Exact, data-free retention by isolating parameters inside a fixed-size network, the same fixed-capacity idea as NSA. Capacity is allocated by weight masks rather than representation directions, and later tasks use earlier weights read-only. It was the strongest method in Continual World (NeurIPS 2021) and is a standard LIBERO lifelong baseline, so reviewers will expect it as a comparison.
papers.setting: supervised vision, task-incremental; later used in continual RL (Continual World) and imitation (LIBERO)

searches.notes:
Plain answer: I did not find the same idea. No paper I could confirm adds per-task modules whose outputs are summed into ONE vector read by every task head and projected into the null space of all earlier heads' weight rows. I searched continual vision, continual/lifelong RL, robot imitation/VLA and LLM continual learning.

The near misses fall into three groups:
(a) Freeze-and-add methods that hide new features from old heads by keeping them apart: new coordinates plus masks (Ternary Feature Masks), separate columns (PNN, CompoNet), or one forward path per task (side-tuning, residual adapters, TAIL, Progressive Prompts).
(b) Methods that use a readout or output null space only approximately (Chaudhry 2020, Duncker 2020), plus the PNAS 2026 theory.
(c) Two weak 2026 LLM preprints, not listed:
- Brainstacks (https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01152) projects a new adapter stack's output away from a sampled SVD subspace of the frozen stacks' outputs.
- AURA (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05219) adds a soft orthogonality penalty between per-task LoRA B matrices.
Neither protects what old heads read, and neither is exact.

Honest reviewer view: novelty is thin.

1) Exact, data-free retention at every closed-loop state is not a contribution. Every freeze-and-add method has it (PNN, side-tuning, TFM, PackNet, CompoNet, TAIL, residual adapters). For one new skill, NSA is side-tuning/PNN with a linear head, as you already suspected.

2) The projection is the only new piece, and your architecture does not need it for exactness. Your adapters read only the raw input and frozen trunk layer 2. So under NSA, head j already outputs W_j h_j, where h_j = h0 + sum over i<=j of the projected writes. Now drop the projection and let head j read its own prefix, h0+g1+...+gj:
- It is exact bitwise, not just to float precision.
- It is still one forward pass (cumulative sums).
- It uses no dims per skill, so there is no ~31-skill cap at 8/256.
- The adapter can write into the copied head's row space, which is the fastest way to change the new head's output. That also removes your zero-init problem (LoRA-style one-zero-factor init works).
This is PNN / side-tuning / Progressive Prompts in residual form, and a reviewer can propose it in one line. Run this ablation before committing. If the prefix version is as good or better, the projection is a cost, not a contribution.

The projection only becomes necessary if something must read ONE vector across skills: a shared critic or value, a skill selector or termination head, a shared nonlinear action expert, or blending heads during skill transitions. If you build that consumer, it is your story.

3) Your Pick->Stack result (exact retention; 1.13-1.30M steps vs 1.50M for full fine-tuning) repeats what TAIL, side-tuning and the PPO LoRA-library preprint already report: adapter about equal to full fine-tuning, with no forgetting. Head-only and KL distillation are weak comparators. RSS reviewers will ask for PNN/side-tuning, LoRA per skill, PackNet and CompoNet.

4) The more defensible contribution may be empirical. Approximate protection (first-order/Kronecker as in Duncker; GPM/InfLoRA-style input-space) fails in closed loop: forgetting concentrates after the grasp and compounds. Input-space blocking also cannot learn a skill that lives inside the old skill's subspace. This fits known evidence (isolation beats regularisation in Continual World/LIBERO; PNAS anterograde interference). A careful manipulation-specific analysis would be new.

5) The random-init subtlety has precedent. LoRA initialises one factor to zero and the other randomly. Plasticity injection (Nikishin et al., NeurIPS 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15555) adds a random head minus its frozen copy so outputs are unchanged at injection.

6) RSS readers hear 'null space' as task-priority control, e.g. Saveriano, An, Lee, ICRA 2015, incremental null-space motion primitives (DOI 10.1109/ICRA.2015.7139694). Define the term carefully or rename it.

Checked and not closer: HAT, Piggyback, SupSup, CPG, Expert Gate, DEN (masks, pruning, experts or expansion with task-conditioned paths); AdapterCL (per-task residual adapters with perplexity routing); CoTASP (ICML 2023, sparse-prompted sub-networks of a meta-policy); CSP (ICLR 2023, subspace of policies); LIBERO and Continual World (benchmarks only); O-LoRA, VPT-NSP, NuSA-CL (input-side or parameter null spaces, approximate); OrthoSkillVLA (PRCV 2026, gradient-subspace constraints plus MoE skill experts).

Not confirmed, so not listed: an OpenReview submission titled 'CNSP: Consistent Null-Space Projection for Principled Prompt-Based Continual Learning'. Its snippet mentions 'head preservation' conditions, but a bot check blocked the page.

All 15 listed entries were checked against arXiv, proceedings or DOI pages. CLARE's RA-L acceptance comes from its arXiv comments field. The PPO LoRA-library paper is an unreviewed June 2026 preprint.

verdict.correct_citation: Marc Masana, Tinne Tuytelaars, Joost van de Weijer. "Ternary Feature Masks: Zero-Forgetting for Task-Incremental Learning." CVPR Workshops 2021 (CLVision), pp. 3570-3579, doi:10.1109/CVPRW53098.2021.00396. arXiv:2001.08714 (v1 23 Jan 2020, v2 21 Apr 2021). Code: github.com/mmasana/TernaryFeatureMasks. The searcher's citation and link are correct. I checked them against the arXiv record, mlanthology and the full v2 PDF, including the equations and appendix.
verdict.what_it_does:
Setting: supervised, task-incremental image classification with the task ID given at test time. AlexNet and VGG-16 are trained from scratch on 4-task Flowers, CUB and Actions, and on 10-task Tiny ImageNet and ImageNet. There is no RL or robotics.

Growth: the network starts narrower than the reference net. For each new task, every layer gains N new features (Alg. S1). The growth rate is picked on the current task's validation set; ImageNet uses 55% for the first task, then +5% per task, capped at the reference size.

Masks: each feature gets a ternary activation mask for each task:
- normal: the new features, used in the forward pass and trained;
- forward-only: earlier tasks' features, used but frozen;
- masked: features added after task s, zeroed whenever task s is evaluated.

Equations: the forward pass is y = (W x) * n^{t,l} (elementwise), where n is the cumulative mask over tasks s <= t. The backward pass is Eq. 6: dL/dW_ij = (m_i OR m_j) x_j dL/dy_i. Only old->old weights are frozen. Every connection that touches a new feature is trained, including weights from new inputs into old outputs (Fig. 3: all unused connections can now be learned without forgetting).

What follows: in task t's forward pass, the new features read the old features and also add into them, at every layer. Old tasks never see either effect, because their own forward pass zeroes the new features.

Extras: task-specific feature normalization x_hat = gamma_t*x + beta_t (2 floats per feature per task) re-tunes frozen features for the new task. Each task has its own head.

Results: forgetting is exactly (0.0) for every TFM entry in all tables. Overhead is 2 bits + 2 floats per feature per task. The authors state that the forward pass depends on the task, so using it without a task ID would need one pass per task. The paper has no null space, no orthogonal projection and no single readout vector shared by all tasks.

Corrections to the searcher:
- It missed the trainable new->old connections, which make TFM closer to NSA's "additive write that old tasks cannot see" than it said.
- Zero forgetting comes from the masks plus the frozen old->old weights. Per-task normalization and per-task heads are add-ons stored per task, not the source of the guarantee.
verdict.exact_delta: TFM already gives NSA's guarantee and most of what it does: old weights are frozen, the new task reads and even adds into existing features, per-task heads read old plus new features, and forgetting is exactly zero with no stored data. It hides the new writes by masking per task, though: each task runs its own forward pass with later features zeroed, and the network widens with every task. What NSA does that TFM does not: every head reads one fixed-width 256-d vector in a single pass that does not depend on the task, and the new write is hidden by projecting it onto the null space of the stacked old linear heads, so each skill costs 8 readout dimensions rather than the adapter's width; NSA also copies the nearest old head as the new head's starting point and starts the adapter random rather than zero, and it is tested on RL policies in closed loop. What TFM does that NSA does not: it grows and writes new->old at every layer with no constraint, and it re-tunes frozen features with per-task gamma/beta, so its new-task write is strictly less constrained than NSA's projected one; the consequence is that when the task ID is known, masking or plain prefix routing (head j reads h_0 + sum_{i<=j} g_i) already keeps old skills exact with no projection, NSA's only distinct contribution is keeping one vector for all heads (which the paper must show matters), and "exact zero-forgetting skill addition" is not new.

verified.title: Progressive Neural Networks
verified.authors: Andrei A. Rusu, Neil C. Rabinowitz, Guillaume Desjardins, Hubert Soyer, James Kirkpatrick, Koray Kavukcuoglu, Razvan Pascanu, Raia Hadsell
verified.mechanism: Each new task adds a full new network column. Earlier columns are frozen. The new column receives lateral connections, through small nonlinear 'adapters', from the hidden layers of every earlier column. Each task has its own output layer reading its own column.
verified.overlap: Already has: frozen old modules, exact retention at every state with no stored data, the new skill reading old features, and later skills reusing all earlier features (the skill-chain property). Missing: the single shared fixed-width vector, the null-space projection and the head-copy initialisation. Width and parameters grow per task, and lateral parameters grow quadratically.

verdict.correct_citation: Andrei A. Rusu*, Neil C. Rabinowitz*, Guillaume Desjardins*, Hubert Soyer, James Kirkpatrick, Koray Kavukcuoglu, Razvan Pascanu, Raia Hadsell (*equal contribution; Google DeepMind). "Progressive Neural Networks." arXiv preprint arXiv:1606.04671 [cs.LG], 2016. v1 is dated 15 Jun 2016 and the current v4 is dated 22 Oct 2022. arXiv lists no journal or conference, so cite it as an arXiv 2016 preprint. The searcher's citation and link are correct. The robotics follow-up should be cited with it: Rusu, Večerík, Rothörl, Heess, Pascanu, Hadsell, "Sim-to-Real Robot Learning from Pixels with Progressive Nets," 1st Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2017), arXiv:1610.04286.
verdict.what_it_does:
I checked this against the full PDF text (v4).

**Architecture:** Each new task gets a full new column: an L-layer ReLU network with random initialisation, including its own output layer. All earlier columns are frozen; their parameters are "constants for the optimizer". Layer i of column k reads its own layer i-1 plus lateral inputs from layer i-1 of every earlier column (Eq. 1): h_i^(k) = f(W_i^(k) h_{i-1}^(k) + sum_{j<k} U_i^(k:j) h_{i-1}^(j)).

**Adapters (Eq. 2):** In practice the lateral path is a nonlinear "adapter". It takes the concatenated features of all earlier columns, multiplies them by a learned scalar alpha (initialised from {1, 0.1, 0.01}), and passes them through a one-hidden-layer MLP. The MLP's first matrix V reduces the dimension to n_{i-1} (1x1 convolutions in conv layers), then U feeds the result into layer i.

**Outputs and retention:** In RL, the top of column k is task k's policy and value: pi^(k)(a|s) := h_L^(k)(s). The task label picks the column at test time. Laterals run only from old columns to new ones, and old columns are frozen, so new parameters never touch old tasks in the forward pass. The paper calls this "immune to forgetting". Retention is exact at every state, needs no stored data, and the paper contrasts this with distillation, which needs a data reservoir.

**Cost:** Hidden units grow linearly and parameters quadratically with the number of columns (Appendix B). Footnote 1 allows any width per column. A Fisher-sensitivity analysis finds later columns use less and less of their capacity, so pruning or compression is left to future work.

**Experiments:** A3C on discrete-action games only, with no manipulation and no continuous control:
- Pong Soup: 8 variants.
- Atari: chains of up to 3 source games, then 12 target games, with 2 to 4 columns.
- Labyrinth: 8 3D maze tasks.
- Results are area-under-curve transfer scores against four baselines: a single column, fine-tuning the output layer only, full fine-tuning, and a random frozen column. Progressive nets give positive transfer on 8 of 12 Atari targets, and transfer grows with more columns.

**Follow-up (CoRL 2017):** The same architecture was used on a real Jaco arm. The robot columns are narrow and the output layer has no adapters. The new output layer starts as a copy of the old policy: the lateral weights from the old last layer are copied from the old output weights, the weights from the new column are zero, and the rest of the new column is random. It also shows a 3-column skill chain on the real robot: reacher, then a moving-target "conveyor" task.
verdict.exact_delta: Progressive nets already have NSA's main selling points: frozen old modules, one head per task chosen by task label, exact retention at every state with no stored data (closed loop included, because an old column's output depends on no new parameter), and a chain of skills where each new module reads all earlier modules' features (nonlinearly, at every layer, so at least as much reuse as NSA). The sim-to-real follow-up (CoRL 2017) already uses narrow added columns, plain linear connections into the new output layer, and NSA's head-copy start exactly: old-head weights on old features, zero weights on new features, the rest of the new column random. So, unlike the searcher's claim, the head-copy initialisation is not a difference either. What progressive nets lack is NSA's core mechanism: they keep old skills by isolation (old heads never read new features, and new features are appended, so width grows linearly and parameters quadratically), while NSA adds each adapter's output, projected by (I - P_{<k}), into the null space of all earlier linear heads inside one fixed 256-d vector that every head reads (no width growth, but the space left to write shrinks by 8 dims per skill). For one new skill NSA is essentially a constrained re-parameterisation of a narrow progressive column with that head-copy start, so its novelty over this line comes down to the fixed-width shared null-space vector at k >= 3, and it needs a parameter-matched narrow progressive-net baseline (with the same head-copy start) to show that this buys something.

verdict.correct_citation: Jeffrey O. Zhang, Alexander Sax, Amir Zamir, Leonidas Guibas, Jitendra Malik. "Side-Tuning: A Baseline for Network Adaptation via Additive Side Networks." ECCV 2020 (spotlight), Springer LNCS, DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-58580-8_41. arXiv:1912.13503 [cs.LG] (v1 31 Dec 2019; v4 31 Jul 2020). The searcher's title, authors, venue and link are all correct. Checked against the full text of arXiv v4 (16 pp.) and the [mlanthology ECCV 2020 entry](https://mlanthology.org/eccv/2020/zhang2020eccv-sidetuning). There is also an [ECVA page](https://ecva.net/papers/eccv_2020/papers_ECCV/html/1104_ECCV_2020_paper.php) and a project site at sidetuning.berkeley.edu.
verdict.what_it_does:
Side-Tuning adapts a frozen pretrained base B by training a side network S on the same raw input x. B is never updated and can be any black box, even ground-truth curvature. The two are merged only at the output representation, which the paper calls "late fusion": R(x) = alpha*B(x) + (1-alpha)*S(x). Alpha is either learned or annealed as alpha(N) = k/(k+N) (Sec. 3.1). S learns a residual on top of the base representation. It is initialized as a copy of B, by distillation, with a low-energy init (trained not to change the output) or with Xavier init (Sec. 3.1, 4.5). Table 4 compares product, summation, a PNN-style MLP and FiLM as the merge.

For incremental learning (Sec. 3.2) it gives each task a new side network. The loss for task t is ||D_t(alpha_t*B(x_t) + (1-alpha_t)*S_t(x_t)) - y_t||. So task t's representation contains only B and its own S_t, and only its own decoder D_t reads it. S_t and D_t are frozen after task t, so forgetting is impossible by isolation ("no possible catastrophic forgetting"). Task IDs are assumed known.

Experiments:
- iCIFAR: ResNet-44 base, a 4-layer conv side network per task, 10 tasks.
- iTaskonomy: ResNet-50 base, a 5-layer conv side network, 12 tasks.
- On both it beats EWC, PSP, PNN, Piggyback and Residual Adapters on average rank.
- Two-task transfer only: Taskonomy, SQuAD with BERT, and Habitat PointNav trained by behavior cloning and by PPO (10M frames) on top of a curvature or denoising perception base.

There is no projection, null-space or orthogonality constraint anywhere. The paper criticizes PSP's orthogonal subspaces for blocking transfer. Letting later tasks reuse earlier side networks appears only as future work (Sec. 5, "Better forward transfer").
verdict.exact_delta: Side-Tuning already has NSA's retention recipe: a frozen base, one additive side module per task reading the raw input, a new readout per task, known task IDs, and forgetting ruled out by construction. So for one new skill, NSA is Side-Tuning with a plain sum instead of alpha-blending, plus a mid-trunk input tap and a projection that does nothing essential at that point; Side-Tuning even runs PPO in Habitat, but only as two-task transfer from a perception encoder, never keeping an old policy. What NSA adds is one fixed-width vector that every head, old and new, reads, made safe by projecting each adapter's output into the null space of all earlier heads' rows (Side-Tuning sends S_t only to its own decoder D_t and never projects). This lets later heads reuse earlier adapters' features, which Side-Tuning lists only as future work (Sec. 5), and lets any new head start as an exact copy of any old head. In return, Side-Tuning has no shared capacity budget (NSA spends up to 8 of 256 dims per skill, so about 32 skills at most) and needs no white-box base (NSA needs linear heads and access to a hidden layer); it also tests merge operators and initializations on 10- and 12-task benchmarks. The candid caveat: with known skill IDs, exact retention plus reuse also works without any projection if head j reads its own prefix h_j (progressive-network style, zero-init adapter, which also avoids the random-init workaround), so the projection is not what delivers retention, and NSA's novelty over Side-Tuning and PNN holds only if experiments show this no-projection prefix variant does worse or lacks something the shared vector gives.

papers.title: Keep Moving: identifying task-relevant subspaces to maximise plasticity for newly learned tasks
papers.authors: Daniel Anthes, Sushrut Thorat, Peter König, Tim C. Kietzmann
papers.mechanism: Splits a shared hidden layer's activation space into the 'readout range' of an old task (row space of that task's linear readout weights, taken from an SVD of the readout) and its null space; any change inside the null space leaves that task's output unchanged. The paper uses this mainly as a diagnostic for EWC, SI, LwF, GEM and replay. It also projects hidden-layer weight gradients with A = alpha*CC^T + beta*NN^T: with alpha=0 the old mapping is preserved exactly, but only in a linear one-hidden-layer network. For deep nonlinear CNNs it switches to a 'functional null space' estimated from old-task gradients, which is approximate and has to be re-estimated during training.
papers.overlap: Shares NSA's core principle exactly: the null space is taken on the OUTPUT side, from the old heads' weights, so it needs no data, and the setting is task-incremental with one head per task. It does not add parameters or an adapter. It projects weight updates rather than an additive post-activation residual, so exactness is lost once a nonlinearity sits between the update and the readout. It has no skill chain, no RL and no closed-loop evaluation. This is the paper a reviewer will cite for 'change in the null space of old readouts does not affect old tasks'.
papers.setting: Supervised: a toy linear network plus Split CIFAR-10 with a CNN. Task-incremental, multi-head.

papers.title: Continual Learning in Low-rank Orthogonal Subspaces
papers.authors: Arslan Chaudhry, Naeemullah Khan, Puneet K. Dokania, Philip H. S. Torr
papers.mechanism: Each task reads the last hidden layer through its own fixed, random, rank-r projection P_t = O_t O_t^T, with P_t^T P_k = 0 for t != k, generated offline before training. Each task's head therefore sees a mutually orthogonal slice of the shared feature, and gradients at that layer are orthogonal across tasks. Lower layers are kept near-isometric by training on the Stiefel manifold (Cayley retraction), and a tiny episodic replay buffer is used for CIFAR and miniImageNet.
papers.overlap: Partitions the shared last layer per task on the OUTPUT side, like NSA's 'each skill uses up 8 dims'. But the slices are fixed and disjoint, so a new task cannot read old features. The trunk keeps training, so retention is approximate and relies on replay for deep nets. There is no added adapter and no projection of an additive residual into the null space of learned heads.
papers.setting: Supervised vision. Task-incremental with task-id-selected heads, single-pass.

papers.title: Brainstacks: Cross-Domain Cognitive Capabilities via Frozen MoE-LoRA Stacks for Continual LLM Learning
papers.authors: Mohammad R. Abu Ayyash
papers.mechanism: Adds frozen MoE-LoRA 'stacks' that combine additively on a frozen base LLM. While a new stack trains, its output delta at each layer is projected off the top-K (K=32 to 64) principal directions of the frozen stacks' combined output deltas: delta <- delta - delta*P. Those directions come from a (randomized) SVD of deltas recorded on 200-400 validation examples from previous domains. A learned sigmoid meta-router weights the stacks at inference.
papers.overlap: Structurally the closest 'projected additive adapter' found, matching NSA's form h_k = h_{k-1} + (I-P) g_k with a frozen base and frozen earlier adapters. But the subspace is the data-estimated span of the earlier adapters' outputs, not the null space of the downstream readouts. It is approximate and needs samples from old domains. The authors attribute retention mainly to freezing plus routing. LLM only, single author, unreviewed.
papers.setting: LLM continual supervised fine-tuning across domains. Routed rather than task-incremental heads.

papers.title: CNSP: Consistent Null-Space Projection for Principled Prompt-Based Continual Learning
papers.authors: Yunjie Han, Jia Liu, et al. (full author list not verified)
papers.venue_year: ICLR 2026 submission on OpenReview; not found among accepted ICLR 2026 papers
papers.mechanism: Abstract only: OpenReview's bot check blocked the full text. The paper claims that keeping performance on old tasks reduces to two jointly sufficient conditions, feature preservation and head preservation. It derives consistency conditions for the full Transformer parameterization and turns them into a null-space projection rule for prompt updates. It extends VPT-NSP2 (NeurIPS 2024), whose null space is input-side (old tasks' feature covariance), approximate, and applied to prompt gradients.
papers.overlap: 'Head preservation' as an explicit sufficient condition is the closest wording to NSA's output-side guarantee that I found. As far as the abstract shows, though, it is still a projection of prompt-parameter updates in a pretrained ViT, with an approximate null space taken from old features. It has no per-task modules that preserve outputs exactly and no RL. I could not verify how head preservation is enforced.
papers.setting: Supervised vision. Prompt-based class-incremental continual learning with pretrained ViTs.

papers.title: InfLoRA: Interference-Free Low-Rank Adaptation for Continual Learning
papers.authors: Yan-Shuo Liang, Wu-Jun Li
papers.mechanism: For each task it adds a LoRA branch on the attention key and value projections. The down-projection is designed analytically and then frozen: its rows lie in the new task's input span with the old tasks' gradient/input subspace removed, where that subspace is kept GPM-style as stored DualGPM bases. Only the zero-initialised up-projection is trained, and the branch is merged into W after the task.
papers.overlap: Like NSA, it adds parameters and makes the new module 'invisible' to old tasks by construction: old inputs map to roughly zero through the frozen down-projection. It is the INPUT-side mirror of NSA's output-side trick. The null space is approximate (energy threshold 0.95-0.98) and needs stored bases of old-task inputs. Its guarantee only covers inputs in the old-data subspace, so it would not cover new states reached in closed loop. Class-incremental, no RL.
papers.setting: Supervised vision. Class-incremental, exemplar-free, pretrained ViT-B/16.

papers.title: Orthogonal Subspace Learning for Language Model Continual Learning
papers.authors: Xiao Wang, Tianze Chen, Qiming Ge, Han Xia, Rong Bao, Rui Zheng, Qi Zhang, Tao Gui, Xuanjing Huang
papers.mechanism: O-LoRA adds one LoRA (A_t, B_t) per task on W_q and W_v and freezes the earlier LoRAs. A soft penalty lambda1 * sum_i ||A_i^T A_t||^2 (lambda1 = 0.5) pushes the new LoRA's input-side subspace to be orthogonal to the old ones, which serve as a proxy for the old tasks' gradient subspaces. It needs no rehearsal and no task id, and the LoRAs can be merged into W.
papers.overlap: The template for 'orthogonal adapters': per-task added parameters, frozen old modules, orthogonality between subspaces, no data. But the orthogonality is between adapter weight subspaces on the input side and is only a soft penalty. It gives no function-level guarantee, because every LoRA acts on the same activations and the outputs of old tasks still change. Not output-side and not exact.
papers.setting: LLM (T5 and LLaMA) continual learning over text tasks. No task id at inference.

papers.title: OPLoRA: Orthogonal Projection LoRA Prevents Catastrophic Forgetting During Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
papers.authors: Yifeng Xiong, Xiaohui Xie
papers.mechanism: Takes an SVD of each frozen pretrained weight and constrains the LoRA update with a two-sided projection, (I - U_k U_k^T) dW (I - V_k V_k^T). The update is thus orthogonal to the top-k left (output-side) and right (input-side) singular vectors. By construction, the top-k singular triples of the weight are preserved exactly, without any data.
papers.overlap: Data-free and exact, and it includes an output-side projector, which matches two of NSA's selling points. But the exactness is about the dominant spectral directions of each weight, not about the outputs of any downstream head. Function on old tasks is not guaranteed. It is a single PEFT stage with no skill chain and no RL.
papers.setting: LLM parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LLaMA-2 7B, Qwen2.5 7B). Forgetting of pretrained knowledge, not task-incremental.

papers.title: Memory-Free Continual Learning with Null Space Adaptation for Zero-Shot Vision-Language Models
papers.authors: Yujin Jo, Taesup Kim
papers.mechanism: NuSA-CL takes an SVD of each current attention weight (W_q, W_k, W_v, W_o) before every task and treats the low-energy singular directions, those outside the top-rho share of spectral energy, as an 'approximate null space'. The update is dW = U_n M V_n^T with a fixed basis and a trainable, zero-initialised r x r matrix M, merged into W after the task. It uses no past data, features or gradients.
papers.overlap: Represents the 'null-space LoRA' line: data-free, a temporary low-rank module, updates confined to an unused subspace. But the subspace is a property of the weights, not of old heads or old data. The guarantee is only a local bound in parameter space, which the authors say is not a function-level guarantee. Approximate, no RL.
papers.setting: Vision-language model (CLIP ViT-B/16). Task-incremental MTIL plus class-incremental CIFAR-100.

papers.title: AlphaEdit: Null-Space Constrained Knowledge Editing for Language Models
papers.authors: Junfeng Fang, Houcheng Jiang, Kun Wang, Yunshan Ma, Shi Jie, Xiang Wang, Xiangnan He, Tat-Seng Chua
papers.mechanism: Before applying a locate-then-edit weight perturbation, it projects the perturbation onto the null space of the preserved-knowledge keys K0. The projector P = U_hat U_hat^T comes from an SVD of K0 K0^T, dropping eigenvectors with eigenvalue above 1e-2. Following MEMIT, K0 is estimated from 100k random Wikipedia (s,r,o) triplets. In theory (W + dW P) K0 = W K0, so outputs for preserved keys are unchanged.
papers.overlap: Same logic of making the change invisible to whatever must be preserved. But the null space is input-side (keys), approximate (eigenvalue threshold) and needs a large sample of preserved data, and it constrains a weight edit. It adds no parameters and has no head or readout structure.
papers.setting: LLM knowledge editing with sequential edits. Not task-incremental.

papers.title: Mitigating the Safety Alignment Tax with Null-Space Constrained Policy Optimization
papers.authors: Yifan Niu, Han Xiao, Dongyi Liu, Nuo Chen, Jia Li
papers.mechanism: NSPO is GRPO-style safety RL for LLMs. Each linear layer's policy gradient is right-multiplied by P = U_hat U_hat^T, an approximate null space of K K^T built from that layer's inputs on 1,000 general-task samples (common sense, math, code), with eigenvalues above 5e-4 removed, as in AlphaEdit. The KL penalty is dropped. It adds no trainable parameters but stores a d x d projector per layer.
papers.overlap: The only policy-optimisation method in this list, so 'null space plus policy gradient' is already published. But its null space is input-side, approximate and built from general-task data, and it constrains weight updates, which is the same family as your failed GPM-style baseline. It is not output-side, not exact and not additive.
papers.setting: RL (GRPO) fine-tuning of LLMs for safety. Not task-incremental.

papers.title: Continual Learning with Scaled Gradient Projection
papers.authors: Gobinda Saha, Kaushik Roy
papers.mechanism: SGP extends GPM. Gradients are projected orthogonal to bases of the old tasks' input representations (SVD with a threshold), but steps along each basis are still allowed in proportion to 1 minus that basis's importance, which relaxes strict orthogonality to recover plasticity. It includes continual RL: PPO on six sequential Atari games, in the BLIP setup. It reports that GPM/SGP-projected gradients passed into Adam lose their projection and cause catastrophic forgetting, and fixes this by projecting Adam's output instead ('Adam-GP').
papers.overlap: Input-side, approximate, stores bases, constrains updates, adds no parameters. It matters to you as the direct precedent for gradient projection in on-policy RL. Its Adam finding is a confound for your 'first-order protection fails in closed loop' baselines: if they projected before Adam, rerun them with the projection after Adam.
papers.setting: Supervised vision (task-incremental, multi-head) plus continual RL (PPO on Atari).

papers.title: Gradient Projection Memory for Continual Learning
papers.authors: Gobinda Saha, Isha Garg, Kaushik Roy
papers.mechanism: After each task, an SVD of each layer's input activations gives bases of the old representation subspace. Bases are kept up to an energy threshold and stored in memory, and new-task gradients are projected orthogonal to them. In the multi-head setup the task-specific head layer is not projected.
papers.overlap: Input-side and approximate (threshold). It uses old-task activations once and then stores bases, not data. It constrains weight updates and adds no parameters. This is the 'GPM-style input-space blocking' you found cannot learn a new skill that lies inside the old skill's subspace.
papers.setting: Supervised vision. PMNIST single-head; CIFAR-100, miniImageNet and 5-Datasets task-incremental multi-head.

papers.title: Training Networks in Null Space of Feature Covariance for Continual Learning
papers.authors: Shipeng Wang, Xiaorong Li, Jian Sun, Zongben Xu
papers.mechanism: Adam-NSCL keeps, for each layer, the uncentered covariance of the previous tasks' layer inputs, updated incrementally. Its approximate null space is the set of singular vectors with singular value at most a * lambda_min (a between 10 and 50). Each Adam update is projected into that null space layer by layer.
papers.overlap: Input-side, approximate, needs covariance statistics of old data, constrains updates, adds no parameters. Like NSA, each task has its own classifier that is frozen after its task, but the heads are never used to define a null space.
papers.setting: Supervised vision. Task-incremental multi-head (10- and 20-split CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet).

papers.title: TRGP: Trust Region Gradient Projection for Continual Learning
papers.authors: Sen Lin, Li Yang, Deliang Fan, Junshan Zhang
papers.mechanism: For each layer it selects the old tasks most related to the new one (a 'trust region', measured by the norm of the gradient projected onto old input subspaces). It reuses their frozen weights through a scaled weight projection with a learnable scaling matrix per task and layer. The shared weights still move only orthogonally to the old input subspaces, as in GPM.
papers.overlap: Input-side, approximate, stores bases. It is the GPM-family method that adds per-task parameters (scaling matrices stored for every task) to get forward transfer from old tasks, a motivation similar to NSA's new head reading old features. It has no output-side projection.
papers.setting: Supervised vision. Task-incremental multi-head.

papers.title: Continual learning of context-dependent processing in neural networks
papers.authors: Guanxiong Zeng, Yang Chen, Bo Cui, Shan Yu
papers.mechanism: Orthogonal Weights Modification (OWM) multiplies each layer's weight update by a projector P = I - A(A^T A + alpha*I)^-1 A^T, kept up to date recursively (RLS-style) from the inputs that layer saw in earlier tasks. Updates are therefore approximately orthogonal to the old input space, with alpha controlling how strictly. A separate context-dependent processing module gates features by context so one classifier can be reused across contexts.
papers.overlap: Input-side, approximate (alpha), stores one P per layer rather than data, constrains updates, adds no parameters apart from the context module. It started the projection family that NSA's input-side baselines belong to, and has nothing on the output side.
papers.setting: Supervised vision. Class-incremental single-head plus context-dependent tasks.

searches.notes:
Bottom line: I did not find the same idea. No paper I could confirm, in continual learning, model editing or RL, adds a post-activation adapter whose output is projected into the null space of the union of frozen linear heads, with one fixed-width vector read by every head, exact data-free retention that also holds in closed loop, and a chain of skills. But the mechanism is thin, and two things will be cited against it.

(1) The output-side principle is already published. Anthes et al. (CoLLAs 2024, first entry):
- They define each old task's readout range and null space from its head weights.
- They state that change in the null space leaves old outputs unchanged.
- They project hidden-layer weight updates into that null space. This is exact and data-free only in a linear one-hidden-layer net; for deep nets they fall back to a data-estimated 'functional null space'.

The same concept is the 'output-null space' of motor cortex: Kaufman, Churchland, Ryu & Shenoy, Nature Neuroscience 17:440-448 (2014), doi:10.1038/nn.3643. Robotics reviewers will also map it onto classical task-priority null-space control. In addition, ORTHOG-SUBSPACE already gives each task its own orthogonal slice of the shared last layer, and CNSP names 'head preservation' as a sufficient condition.

NSA's genuine but small delta over Anthes et al.: it projects an additive residual applied after the nonlinearity, not a weight update. That keeps the output-side guarantee exact in a deep nonlinear policy without any data.

(2) My own analysis, not from any paper: NSA is a reparameterisation of expansion. Take the concatenation [h; g_k] and fix every old head's weights on g_k at zero (Progressive Nets, Rusu et al., arXiv 1606.04671; side-tuning; DEN-style growth). That gives the same exact, data-free, closed-loop retention for any chain length. Every NSA head k equals a concat head with tied weights W_k^b = W_k(I - P_{<k}). So concatenation is at least as expressive and has no 8-dims-per-skill budget; NSA runs out after about 31 new 8-dim skills in 256 dims. The null-space projection therefore buys nothing by construction at k >= 3. You need a width-matched concat/PNN baseline on a chain of 3 or more skills, showing that the shared vector helps (sample efficiency or transfer). Otherwise reviewers will call the projection cosmetic. Also, starting the adapter random rather than zero is the standard LoRA/ControlNet asymmetry (one factor zero, the other random), not a contribution.

How the methods you named classify:
- Input side, approximate, needs old-data statistics, constrains weight updates: OWM, GPM, TRGP (adds per-task scaling matrices), SGP, Adam-NSCL, AdNS, VPT-NSP2, AlphaEdit, NSPO, NESS and LoRA-Null. The null space comes from old features, keys or gradient bases with an eigenvalue or energy threshold, and the statistics are stored bases, stored covariances or data samples.
  - AdNS: Kong et al., ECCV 2022, arXiv 2207.12061; low-rank approximate null space plus intra-task distillation.
  - VPT-NSP2: Lu et al., NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2406.05658; prompt-gradient projection with consistency conditions for attention and LayerNorm.
  - NESS: Pham et al., CPAL 2026, arXiv 2602.21919.
  - LoRA-Null: Tang et al., AAAI 2026, arXiv 2503.02659.
  - Of these, InfLoRA, NESS and LoRA-Null add or merge low-rank modules placed in that input-side null space.
- Data-free, but only a weight-space constraint with no function-level guarantee:
  - O-LoRA: soft orthogonality between LoRA subspaces.
  - NuSA-CL: low-energy directions of the weight spectrum.
  - OPLoRA: exact only for the top-k singular triples.
  - NUFILT: Qiu et al., ICLR 2026, arXiv 2509.21413; uses task vectors as stand-ins for input subspaces in data-free merging.
- No null space at all: MagMax (Marczak et al., ECCV 2024, arXiv 2407.06322) is sequential fine-tuning plus max-magnitude merging; approximate, needs no old data.
- Others checked: OA-Adapter (Wan et al., arXiv 2505.22358) is another orthogonal-subspace adapter for LLMs, unreviewed. FFNB (Sahbi & Zhan, arXiv 2111.11366) combines expansion with an input-side approximate null space.

None of these is both output-side and exact.

Checks before you claim 'exact' and 'first-order protection fails':
(a) The heads must read h with no LayerNorm or nonlinearity after the adapters.
(b) Any running observation or return normalisation shared across skills must be frozen for old skills, or exactness breaks.
(c) Per-skill critics that read the shared vector are not protected unless their rows are added to P. This does not affect behaviour, but it matters if you ever resume training an old skill.
(d) SGP (AAAI 2023) found that GPM/SGP-projected gradients passed through Adam cause catastrophic forgetting under PPO, and fixed it by projecting Adam's output. If your Kronecker or GPM baselines projected before Adam, rerun them before a reviewer asks.

The 'input-side blocking cannot learn the new skill' result is expected, not novel: TRGP, SGP, AdNS and Anthes et al. all exist because strict input-side null spaces kill plasticity when tasks share subspaces.

Positioning for RSS: the honest pitch is an empirical closed-loop finding plus a minimal exact mechanism, not a new null-space method. The finding is that approximate or first-order protection fails after the grasp and compounds, while an exact data-free guarantee costs about 25% extra parameters and still learns faster than full fine-tuning. Cite Anthes et al. and the expansion methods up front, and win on the chain experiment. Also expect the counter-narrative from Hu et al., 'Simple Recipe Works: Vision-Language-Action Models are Natural Continual Learners with Reinforcement Learning' (RLC 2026, arXiv 2603.11653). They report that sequential LoRA fine-tuning with on-policy RL shows little or no forgetting in large VLAs.

Access caveat: CNSP's full text sits behind OpenReview's browser verification. I did not bypass it, so its entry rests only on the abstract as quoted in search results. I also could not find CNSP among accepted ICLR 2026 papers.

Keep Moving: Identifying Task-Relevant Subspaces to Maximise Plasticity for Newly Learned Tasks. Proceedings of the 3rd Conference on Lifelong Learning Agents (CoLLAs 2024), PMLR vol. 274, pp. 815-831; the proceedings volume is dated 2025. arXiv:2310.04741: v1 (7 Oct 2023) had a different title, 'Balancing stability and plasticity in continual learning: the readout-decomposition of activation change (RDAC) framework', so reviewers may cite it as RDAC; v6 is from 20 Jun 2024.
