verdict.what_it_does:
I checked this against the full PDF text. It is mainly a diagnostic paper for task-incremental, multi-head continual learning. Old readouts are frozen, each new task gets its own linear readout, and every readout reads the same last shared hidden layer.

(1) Decomposition. An SVD of a frozen old readout W_R^k gives an orthonormal basis C for its range and a basis N for its null space in the pre-readout activation space. Because NN^T W_R^T = 0, any activation change in the null space cannot change that task's output. The bases come from the weights alone, need no data and are computed once. The readout range is treated as an upper bound on the space that matters.

(2) Diagnosis. On CIFAR-110 (CIFAR-10, then ten CIFAR-100 splits: 11 tasks, small VGG, 128-d pre-readout layer) and on TinyImageNet (5 tasks, slim ResNet18), the paper measures how far task-1 activations move in the range versus the null space of the task-1 readout under EWC, SI, LwF, GEM and replay. Regularisers suppress movement in both subspaces and lose plasticity; replay and GEM move in both and stay stable. The paper's own projection is not run on these benchmarks.

(3) Algorithm, linear case only. A one-hidden-layer linear network (11 units, no biases, Split MNIST, 2 tasks) is trained with projected gradients: W_H <- W_H + A dW_H, with A = alpha CC^T + beta NN^T. Since W_R1 A = 0 exactly when alpha = 0, this gives exact stability with no loss of plasticity.

(4) Nonlinear case, approximate. The authors state that once nonlinearities are present, the readout-based projection can no longer filter the hidden-layer gradient. For a ReLU VGG CNN on Split CIFAR-10 (2 tasks) they instead estimate a functional range at every layer from gradients of the old task's loss on old-task data. Each estimate uses 20 epochs of old data and an SVD keeping 99.9% of variance; it is redone every 200 steps, and Adam updates are re-projected. Task 1 stays almost, but not exactly, stable. The method needs old data, and the authors present it mainly as an analysis tool.

Appendix A.3 derives, but does not test, nested null-space constraints for a 3-layer linear network (n(k-1) null spaces for k tasks). Appendix A.4 hypothesises, also untested, that leaving room for new features could help forward transfer.

The paper explicitly limits itself to shared networks 'without any changes to the network architecture'. It has no adapters or added parameters, and no RL, robotics or closed-loop evaluation.

The searcher's summary is accurate. Its only omission is that the diagnostic results also cover 11-task CIFAR-110 and 5-task TinyImageNet, while the projection method itself is run only on 2-task problems.
verdict.exact_delta: Anthes et al. already establish the principle NSA relies on: a change to the shared pre-readout vector that lies in the null space of a frozen linear head (computed from that head's SVD, without data) leaves that task's output exactly unchanged, in a task-incremental multi-head network where every head reads the same layer; in their one-hidden-layer linear network, the alpha=0 rule (W_H <- W_H + NN^T dW_H) does the same thing as NSA with a linear adapter folded into the shared weights. What NSA adds is a separate nonlinear module per skill on a frozen trunk, projected after the nonlinearity onto the joint null space of all previous heads, which keeps retention exact in a deep nonlinear network with no data, no re-estimation and any optimiser; this is precisely the case where Anthes et al. say the readout projection breaks and fall back to an approximate, data-dependent, gradient-based null space; NSA also adds skill chains (k>=3) in which later heads read features written by earlier adapters, and PPO with closed-loop retention on ManiSkill3. Conversely, Anthes et al. add no parameters (they explicitly rule out architectural changes), trade stability against plasticity with alpha and beta, mostly diagnose EWC, SI, LwF, GEM and replay over 11 CIFAR tasks, and run their own projection only on 2-task supervised problems. Verdict: this is not NSA, but it is the paper reviewers will cite for the claim that null-space changes do not affect old heads, so NSA's novelty must rest on the exact additive construction after the nonlinearity, the k>=3 chain and the closed-loop RL evidence, not on that principle.

papers.title: Continual learning: a feature extraction formalization, an efficient algorithm, and fundamental obstructions
papers.authors: Binghui Peng, Andrej Risteski
papers.mechanism: Task-incremental setting: a shared feature map R(x)=U^T x with one linear head v_i per environment. Old heads are frozen. Their algorithm, DPGrad, trains U and the new head, but every update of U is projected on both sides as P_{W-perp} grad_U P_{V-perp}. V is the span of the previous heads and W is the span of the previous effective predictors U v_j. Because of the right-hand projection, the shared representation changes only in directions every old head ignores, so old predictions stay exactly fixed for every input. New feature directions are seeded with random Gaussian noise inside that protected complement, because a zero start would stall. They also prove that for nonlinear features in a fixed hypothesis class, no algorithm, efficient or not, can avoid forgetting.
papers.overlap: This is NSA's core principle, published four years earlier. They write new features only in the null space of all previous heads, get exact retention at every input with no stored data, and use a random rather than zero start for the new directions (the same subtlety you hit). What they do not have: deep or nonlinear features (they prove this impossible without growing the model), a frozen trunk with residual adapters, a new head copied from an old head, skill chains, any experiments, or RL and closed-loop control. NSA can honestly be framed as the escape from their impossibility theorem by adding parameters (growth), but not as the principle itself.
papers.setting: supervised (linear regression theory); task-incremental, multi-head

papers.title: Keep moving: identifying task-relevant subspaces to maximise plasticity for newly learned tasks
papers.authors: Daniel Anthes, Sushrut Thorat, Peter König, Tim C. Kietzmann
papers.mechanism: Task-incremental, multi-head networks with a shared backbone. They split the last hidden layer's activity space into the range of the old task's readout (an orthonormal basis from an SVD of the readout weights) and its null space. They show that only activity change inside the old readout's range causes forgetting, while restricting change in the null space only costs plasticity. In a linear one-hidden-layer network, projecting the hidden-layer gradient onto the old readout's null space gives the stability of a frozen model with no loss of plasticity. For deep nonlinear networks they estimate an approximate 'functional null space' per layer from old-task gradients on sampled old data (SVD keeping 99.9% of variance, re-estimated every 200 steps). Projecting into it stabilizes the network almost completely, with a slight drop in plasticity.
papers.overlap: Same decomposition (old-readout range vs null space), same claim that null-space change is free, and an explicit null-space projection experiment. They frame it as an analysis or diagnostic tool, not a method. In deep nets their preservation is approximate and needs old-task data (first-order, gradient-based). There is no architectural adapter on a frozen trunk, no exactness at off-distribution or closed-loop states, no skill chain, and no RL.
papers.setting: supervised classification (Split MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, TinyImageNet); task-incremental, multi-head

papers.title: Order parameters and phase transitions of continual learning in deep neural networks
papers.authors: Haozhe Shan, Qianyi Li, Haim Sompolinsky
papers.mechanism: A statistical-mechanics theory of continual learning in deep, wide networks that compares a shared readout (single-head) with task-specific readouts (multi-head). In the multi-head case they find a regime where hidden representations do change while task 2 is learned, but the changes stay inside the null space of task 1's readout. Forgetting is then exactly zero. The same regime comes with poor generalization on the new task, which they call 'catastrophic anterograde interference'. They suggest null-space confinement as one way the brain could limit interference.
papers.overlap: Theory for why changes in a readout's null space leave that head exactly intact, plus a warning that confining learning there can cost new-task generalization. Here the confinement emerges from the training regime; it is not a designed mechanism. No adapters, no growth, no RL. Useful to cite. Your sample-efficiency numbers are evidence against the anterograde cost in your setting.
papers.setting: supervised theory; task-incremental multi-head vs single-head

papers.title: Learning leaves a memory trace in motor cortex
papers.authors: Darby M. Losey, Jay A. Hennig, Emily R. Oby, Matthew D. Golub, Patrick T. Sadtler, Kristin M. Quick, Stephen I. Ryu, Elizabeth C. Tyler-Kabara, Aaron P. Batista, Byron M. Yu, Steven M. Chase
papers.mechanism: Monkeys controlling a cursor through a brain-computer interface learned a new decoder and then returned to the familiar one. While they used the familiar decoder again, M1 activity kept a lasting 'memory trace' of the new learning. The trace sat mainly in the familiar decoder's output-null dimensions; its output-potent component was not significant. So the old behaviour was performed proficiently while the trace persisted. The authors propose that such traces allow several behaviours to be learned jointly without interference, and support faster relearning.
papers.overlap: The biological counterpart of NSA's principle: information about the new skill is stored where the old readout cannot see it, and the old skill is preserved. It is empirical neuroscience, not an algorithm: the decoders are fixed by the experimenters and preservation is only approximate. A good motivating citation for an output-null framing.
papers.setting: neuroscience (macaque M1, BCI learning); not ML

papers.title: A general framework for managing multiple tasks in highly redundant robotic systems
papers.authors: Bruno Siciliano, Jean-Jacques E. Slotine
papers.venue_year: ICAR 1991 (5th Int. Conf. on Advanced Robotics), pp. 1211-1216
papers.mechanism: Task-priority redundancy resolution for redundant manipulators. A lower-priority task's command is passed through the null-space projector (I - J^+ J) of the higher-priority tasks' Jacobians. The recursion extends to many tasks with nested null spaces, so higher-priority task outputs are exactly unaffected by lower-priority ones.
papers.overlap: Same algebra as NSA: h_k = h_{k-1} + (I - P_{<k}) g_k with nested null spaces amounts to strict priority for old skills. Here it is applied to joint commands with known Jacobians, not to a learned feature vector read by learned heads, and nothing is learned. RSS reviewers will recognise the formula immediately. Better to cite it yourself, for example as 'task-priority control moved from joint space into the policy's feature space', than to have a reviewer point it out.
papers.setting: robot control (no learning)

papers.title: A Neural Population Mechanism for Rapid Learning
papers.authors: Matthew G. Perich, Juan A. Gallego, Lee E. Miller
papers.mechanism: During curl-field reach adaptation, planning activity in premotor cortex (PMd) changed in the output-null subspace of the PMd-to-M1 mapping. The output-potent mapping, which carries what PMd sends to M1, stayed stable. The authors propose this as a population-level way to adapt quickly without rewiring the connections between areas.
papers.overlap: Learning is written into the null space of a downstream readout while that readout's channel is preserved. Descriptive neuroscience about a single adaptation; not about keeping several skills or about an algorithm.
papers.setting: neuroscience (macaque PMd/M1, visuomotor adaptation)

papers.title: Cortical activity in the null space: permitting preparation without movement
papers.authors: Matthew T. Kaufman, Mark M. Churchland, Stephen I. Ryu, Krishna V. Shenoy
papers.mechanism: Introduces the split of population activity into output-null and output-potent parts relative to a linear readout to muscles. Preparatory activity in motor cortex changes along dimensions that cancel at the readout, which allows preparation without movement. At movement onset, activity enters output-potent dimensions.
papers.overlap: The origin of the 'compute in readout-invisible directions' idea and of the terminology. It does not address learning, continual learning or multiple skills. The 2024 review by Churchland and Shenoy ('Preparatory activity and the expansive null-space', Nat Rev Neurosci 25:213-236) surveys the follow-up work.
papers.setting: neuroscience (macaque motor cortex)

papers.title: Elastic Feature Consolidation for Cold Start Exemplar-Free Incremental Learning
papers.authors: Simone Magistri, Tomaso Trinci, Albin Soutif-Cormerais, Joost van de Weijer, Andrew D. Bagdanov
papers.mechanism: Exemplar-free class-incremental learning. Feature drift is penalised with a quadratic form built from an Empirical Feature Matrix: the expected outer product of the gradients of the log-probabilities with respect to the features, which measures how sensitive the classifier is to each feature direction. The paper reports that the matrix's rank equals the number of classes seen. Drift along directions the old classifier is insensitive to is almost unpenalised (only a small damping term applies), while drift along sensitive directions is penalised. Gaussian prototypes correct task-recency bias.
papers.overlap: This is the 'feature-space constraint aligned with old-head sensitivity' idea: features may move where the old classifier cannot see. But the constraint is a soft regulariser estimated on current-task data, preservation is approximate, there is a single head (class-incremental), no architectural guarantee and no RL. It is the closest thing I found to 'classifier-null-space distillation'.
papers.setting: supervised vision; class-incremental, exemplar-free

papers.title: Continual Learning in Low-rank Orthogonal Subspaces
papers.authors: Arslan Chaudhry, Naeemullah Khan, Puneet K. Dokania, Philip H. S. Torr
papers.mechanism: Task-incremental and multi-head (ORTHOG-SUBSPACE). Before each task head, the shared last-layer features pass through a fixed task-specific projector onto one of several mutually orthogonal low-rank subspaces. The projectors come from a random orthonormal basis split into disjoint blocks of rank m/T, computed offline. Earlier layers are kept orthonormal by optimising on the Stiefel manifold, so gradients from different tasks stay nearly orthogonal. A small replay buffer is used on CIFAR and miniImageNet.
papers.overlap: Each task reads its own slice of one shared feature vector, which resembles NSA heads each using 8 dimensions. But the trunk is still trained on every task, so retention is approximate (reported forgetting is non-zero). Subspaces must be allocated in advance, and a new head cannot read the features of earlier tasks. Nothing is projected relative to old heads' weights.
papers.setting: supervised classification; task-incremental, multi-head

papers.title: Cortical preparatory activity indexes learned motor memories
papers.authors: Xulu Sun, Daniel J. O'Shea, Matthew D. Golub, Eric M. Trautmann, Saurabh Vyas, Stephen I. Ryu, Krishna V. Shenoy
papers.mechanism: During curl-field learning, preparatory activity changed inside the force-predictive subspace, where existing patterns were reassociated with new movements. Activity also shifted uniformly, for all reach directions, along a dimension orthogonal to that subspace. During washout, the force-predictive changes reverted but the orthogonal shift persisted, indexing a retained motor memory that supports faster relearning.
papers.overlap: A learned skill's memory is kept in dimensions orthogonal to the output-relevant subspace: a biological analogue of storing skill-specific features where the current readout ignores them. Descriptive; no algorithm and no exact preservation.
papers.setting: neuroscience (macaque motor/premotor cortex, force-field adaptation)

papers.title: Organizing recurrent network dynamics by task-computation to enable continual learning
papers.authors: Lea Duncker, Laura N. Driscoll, Krishna V. Shenoy, Maneesh Sahani, David Sussillo
papers.mechanism: Continual multitask learning in RNNs. Each recurrent weight update is projected on both sides: on the right by the complement of the previous tasks' input/activity covariance, and on the left by the complement of the previous tasks' recurrent output-activation covariance. Both are soft, regularised projectors computed from stored covariances, and the readout updates are projected the same way. New tasks' dynamics then move into orthogonal subspaces, while similar tasks can share subspaces.
papers.overlap: This is essentially the two-sided (Kronecker-style), first-order weight-update projection you already found fails in closed loop. Protection is approximate and defined by data covariances, not by the null space of the readout weights. No adapters and no exact guarantee; neuroscience-style supervised tasks.
papers.setting: supervised RNN cognitive tasks; sequential multitask (task-incremental via rule inputs)

papers.title: Superposition of many models into one
papers.authors: Brian Cheung, Alex Terekhov, Yubei Chen, Pulkit Agrawal, Bruno Olshausen
papers.mechanism: Stores many task models in one parameter set by binding each task's weights to a random task-specific context (a random sign vector, random phases, or a random rotation): W = sum_k W_k C_k^{-1}. To retrieve task k, the weights are multiplied by C_k. The other tasks then appear as zero-mean, nearly orthogonal noise whose size grows with (K-1)/M, where K is the number of tasks and M the dimension. Retrieval is approximate.
papers.overlap: Interference is avoided through near-orthogonality in high dimensions, in parameter space. It is neither the readout null space nor exact. Shares only the intuition that tasks can occupy non-interfering directions of a shared space.
papers.setting: supervised and RL (online, non-stationary tasks); task identity known

papers.title: Engineering flexible machine learning systems by traversing functionally invariant paths
papers.authors: Guruprasad Raghavan, Bahey Tharwat, Surya Narayanan Hari, Dhruvil Satani, Rex Liu, Matt Thomson
papers.mechanism: Treats weight space as a Riemannian manifold with metric g = J^T J, where J is the Jacobian of the outputs on prior-task data. Each step moves the weights in the direction that changes those outputs least, while a weighted secondary loss pulls toward a new goal (a new task, sparsity or robustness). The resulting paths are approximately function-preserving.
papers.overlap: An output-null move in parameter space, but soft, first-order and tied to old-task data. This is the class of methods your closed-loop results argue drifts once the policy reaches states outside that data. No architectural guarantee.
papers.setting: supervised vision and NLP (CNNs, ViT, BERT); sequential tasks

papers.title: Motor cortex signals for each arm are mixed across hemispheres and neurons yet partitioned within the population response
papers.authors: Katherine C. Ames, Mark M. Churchland
papers.mechanism: Most motor cortex neurons respond during movement of either arm, but at the population level each arm's activity lies in its own orthogonal subspace. A linear decoder of one arm's muscles therefore naturally ignores the activity related to the other arm.
papers.overlap: A biological example of one shared population read by several readouts, each blind to the others' subspaces. This is the structure NSA builds for skill chains (k >= 3). Descriptive only.
papers.setting: neuroscience (macaque motor cortex, bimanual cycling)

papers.title: Learning by neural reassociation
papers.authors: Matthew D. Golub, Patrick T. Sadtler, Emily R. Oby, Kristin M. Quick, Stephen I. Ryu, Elizabeth C. Tyler-Kabara, Aaron P. Batista, Steven M. Chase, Byron M. Yu
papers.mechanism: In short-term learning of a perturbed brain-computer-interface decoder, monkeys did not create new activity patterns. They kept a fixed repertoire and re-associated existing patterns with new movements, which is suboptimal. This extends Sadtler et al. 2014 (Nature 512:423-426), who found that decoder perturbations inside the 'intrinsic manifold' are learned much more easily than perturbations outside it.
papers.overlap: The opposite strategy to NSA: the readout or association changes while no new features are added, closer to your head-only baseline (which was the slowest). Useful contrast, not the same idea.
papers.setting: neuroscience (macaque M1, BCI learning)

searches.notes:
I did find the same core idea. NSA cannot claim "write new features where the old readouts cannot see them", or "exact retention through the readout null space", as its contribution. I did not find NSA's specific construction or any robotics/RL use of it.

1. Who already has the principle:
- Peng & Risteski (NeurIPS 2022): shared features plus one frozen linear head per task. Feature updates are right-multiplied by the projector onto the complement of all previous heads, so old predictions are exactly unchanged for every input. New directions start from random noise inside that complement, which is the same "random, not zero" subtlety you hit. Their setting is linear-feature theory, and they prove that for nonlinear features nothing can avoid forgetting without growing the model.
- Anthes et al. (CoLLAs 2024, task-incremental multi-head): split hidden activity into old-readout range vs null space, show that only range changes cause forgetting, and project learning into the readout null space. This is exact in linear nets; in deep nets it is approximate and needs old-task gradients.
- Shan, Li & Sompolinsky (PNAS 2026): derive zero forgetting in multi-head networks when representation changes stay in the old readout's null space, and warn that this regime can hurt new-task generalization.
- Neuroscience: "output-null" learning is established. Kaufman 2014 introduced the term, Perich 2018 found learning in output-null dimensions, and Losey 2024 found new learning stored in the old decoder's output-null dimensions while the old skill is retained, explicitly proposed as a way to learn many behaviours without interference.
- Robotics: nested null-space projection for strict task priority (Siciliano & Slotine 1991) is exactly NSA's algebra, applied at the joint level.

2. What I did not find anywhere:
- a frozen deep nonlinear trunk with residual adapters whose outputs are projected onto the joint null space of all previous heads;
- exact retention at every state reached in closed loop, with no stored data;
- a new head initialised as a copy of the nearest old head;
- chains of skills where later skills read earlier adapters' features in one fixed-width vector;
- any RL or robot evaluation.

Recent null-space continual-learning methods (Adam-NSCL, InfLoRA, NSP2, NuSA-CL, AlphaEdit-style editing, IGFA 2026) all project using the input-feature covariance or the weight spectrum, not the readout. Recent VLA continual-learning work uses replay or adapter routing, not null spaces.

3. Honest risk.
- **Concatenation already gives exact retention.** With linear heads, writing g into the null space of the old heads is equivalent, from the old heads' point of view, to appending new coordinates they give zero weight. So progressive nets, side-tuning and DER-style feature concatenation also retain old skills exactly. What NSA adds is a fixed-width vector shared by all heads, in which features overlap. That only matters at k >= 3, and you have not tested it yet.
- **How a reviewer will read k=2.** Anyone who knows Peng & Risteski or Anthes et al. will call the k=2 result "side-tuning with a projector".
- **Where the defensible novelty lies.** Three things: the closed-loop finding (first-order protection of weight updates, i.e. Kronecker/Duncker-style or GPM-style, fails because errors compound after the grasp, while the architectural output-null construction is exact at every state); the sample-efficiency results against fine-tuning and KL distillation; and skill-chain experiments against a concatenation baseline (progressive nets or side-tuning) with matched parameters, showing that the shared vector helps (feature reuse, a fixed interface for a shared critic or downstream module, fewer parameters).
- **Reframing.** Cite Peng & Risteski and frame NSA as the growth-based escape from their impossibility result. Cite Siciliano & Slotine as "task priority in feature space".

4. Naming. "NSA / null-space adapter" collides with NuSA-CL (Jo & Kim, ICLR 2026, "Memory-Free Continual Learning with Null Space Adaptation", a weight-space method). Something like "output-null skill adapters" avoids the clash and uses the neuroscience term.

5. Checked but not the same idea:
- Sadtler 2014 and Golub 2018: short-term BCI learning reuses existing activity patterns, which is closer to head-only learning.
- Hennig et al. 2018 (eLife): output-null activity is constrained, not free.
- Stavisky 2017 (Neuron): feedback signals first enter output-null dimensions.
- Stolfo et al. (NeurIPS 2024): LLM "entropy neurons" write into an effective unembedding null space. It is an emergent mechanism, not a learning method.
- Reservoir computing with several readouts: retention is exact only because the reservoir is frozen, which is head-only.
- Backward-compatible or linear-separability feature constraints: not null-space based.
- I found no "distil only in the old head's row space" method beyond the soft regulariser in EFC (ICLR 2024).

All papers listed were confirmed: author lists and page numbers through Crossref or the proceedings pages, and mechanisms from the full text or abstracts.

verdict.what_it_does:
A theory paper on task-incremental, multi-head, supervised regression.

Model: one fixed-size shared linear representation R(x) = U^T x, with U in R^{d x r}. The number of features r is fixed; the introduction explicitly rules out adding features or growing the model. Each environment gets one scalar linear head v_i in R^r, frozen when its environment ends. No old data is replayed.

DPGrad (Algorithm 1):
- Start of environment i: U <- U + sigma * P_{W-perp} rand(d,r) P_{V-perp}, and v_i <- sigma * rand(r). The new head is fresh and random, not copied.
- Training: plain gradient descent with U <- U - eta * P_{W-perp} grad_U P_{V-perp}. The head step is not projected, so v_i reads the old features (its component in V) and the new ones (its component in V-perp).
- End of environment: w_hat_i = Round_nu(U v_i). Only if ||P_{W-perp} w_hat_i|| >= 1/D do W (in R^d, span of earlier predictors) and V (in R^r, span of earlier heads) each grow by one direction. Then U <- P_W U P_V is applied unconditionally.

Why it works:
- The right projection keeps every change of the shared representation inside the null space of all accepted earlier heads. So U v_j stays exactly unchanged at every input. Their Appendix B proof states U_{i,t} v_j = U_{j,end} v_j.
- The left (input-side) projection keeps U block-diagonal. The loss then splits into fitting the head on frozen old features plus a rank-1 factorization for the new feature. They say the quadratic loss's cross-terms require projecting on both sides, unlike OGD.

Guarantees and caveats:
- Theorem 2.11 assumes isotropic inputs plus norm, signal and bit-complexity conditions. With high probability, every earlier loss stays <= eps during later training and the current loss ends <= eps.
- The headline guarantee is therefore eps-approximate. A task that adds no new direction never enters V; its retention is only bounded by O(sqrt(D) r sigma).
- The random start is justified only as "a good initialization" for a nonconvex factorization (no spectral init, no re-initialization). The paper never argues that a zero start would stall, and with their random head it would not.
- Theorem 2.12: for one fixed nonlinear class (a 2-layer CNN with quadratic activation; ReLU in Appendix C), no proper continual learner, efficient or not, can guarantee error below 1/1000 on both of two environments with probability >= 1/2. The conclusion says improper learners and task-specific representations are not ruled out.

Experiments: arXiv v1 has none, but the NeurIPS camera-ready adds two.
- Synthetic linear: d=100, r=20, k=500 tasks. Mean error is 0.001 for DPGrad, 83.6 for OGD and 5.2 for SGD.
- Appendix E, Rotated and Permuted MNIST: 10 tasks, a 2-layer MLP with 300 hidden units, a shared first layer and per-task 10-class heads. Two variants are tested: DPGrad (linear activation, up to 10 directions per task) and a heuristic DPGrad+ (ReLU; adds the top-15 singular vectors of the weight matrix). DPGrad+ reaches 76.6% / 89.5% mean accuracy with backward transfer -0.04 / -0.01. So for nonlinear features they show approximate, not exact, retention.

verified.mechanism: Task-incremental, multi-head networks with a shared backbone. They split the last hidden layer's activity space into the range of the old task's readout (an orthonormal basis from an SVD of the readout weights) and its null space. They show that only activity change inside the old readout's range causes forgetting, while restricting change in the null space only costs plasticity. In a linear one-hidden-layer network, projecting the hidden-layer gradient onto the old readout's null space gives the stability of a frozen model with no loss of plasticity. For deep nonlinear networks they estimate an approximate 'functional null space' per layer from old-task gradients on sampled old data (SVD keeping 99.9% of variance, re-estimated every 200 steps). Projecting into it stabilizes the network almost completely, with a slight drop in plasticity.
verified.overlap: Same decomposition (old-readout range vs null space), same claim that null-space change is free, and an explicit null-space projection experiment. They frame it as an analysis or diagnostic tool, not a method. In deep nets their preservation is approximate and needs old-task data (first-order, gradient-based). There is no architectural adapter on a frozen trunk, no exactness at off-distribution or closed-loop states, no skill chain, and no RL.
verified.setting: supervised classification (Split MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, TinyImageNet); task-incremental, multi-head

verdict.correct_citation: Daniel Anthes, Sushrut Thorat, Peter König, Tim C. Kietzmann. "Keep moving: identifying task-relevant subspaces to maximise plasticity for newly learned tasks." Proceedings of The 3rd Conference on Lifelong Learning Agents (CoLLAs 2024), PMLR vol. 274, pp. 815-831. The PMLR volume is dated 2025, BibTeX key pmlr-v274-anthes25a. Preprint: arXiv:2310.04741, v1 7 Oct 2023; v6 20 Jun 2024 is the CoLLAs camera-ready, marked "Published at 3rd Conference on Lifelong Learning Agents (CoLLAs), 2024". The searcher's citation is correct, apart from the PMLR year being 2025, not 2024.
verdict.what_it_does:
Checked against the full v6 text. The paper calls itself an analysis or "diagnostic tool", not a method. The setting is task-incremental, multi-head supervised classification: a shared backbone with one linear+softmax readout per task on the last hidden layer.

The core idea: split the pre-readout activation space into the range of an old task's readout W_Rk (an orthonormal basis C from an SVD of W_Rk) and its null space N. Activation change Δh·NNᵀ is invisible to the old readout. So only change in the range can cause forgetting, and restricting change in the null space only costs plasticity.

They use this in three ways.

(1) Diagnostic on 11-task CIFAR-110 (small VGG). They split task-1 pre-readout drift into range and null-space parts for EWC, SI, LwF, replay and GEM. The regularizers shrink both parts, which over-constrains the network. Replay moves in both parts and still stays stable.

(2) A causal test in a one-hidden-layer LINEAR network: 11 hidden units, no biases, 2-task Split MNIST. The hidden-weight gradient is projected as A·ΔW_H with A = αCCᵀ + βNNᵀ. With α=0, W_R1·A = 0 (Eq. 1), so task-1 outputs are unchanged for every input. The projector is computed from W_R1 alone; in their words it works "without any dependence on the task's data". Empirically, stability is "similar" to a fully frozen hidden layer, with no plasticity loss against unconstrained training.

(3) A deep nonlinear network: 5 small VGG blocks (8-32 channels) plus a 64-unit dense layer, on 2-task Split CIFAR-10. The authors state that with nonlinearities the readout-weight projector "cannot be used directly to filter the gradient updates". Instead, per layer, they estimate a "functional range" from gradients of the OLD TASK'S LOSS on old data. The estimate is redone every 200 steps from 20 epochs of old-task data, keeping SVD directions that explain 99.9% of variance. Every layer's weight update is projected onto its complement using a custom re-projecting Adam, in the style of OGD/GPM. This stabilizes "almost completely", plasticity drops slightly, and range drift is not fully stopped. Because it needs old data, they call it useful "primarily as an analysis tool".

What the paper does not do:
- Freeze the backbone for good. All backbone weights keep training; the backbone is frozen only for a 5-10 epoch warm-up of the new readout.
- Use architectural methods. These are explicitly out of scope, and there are no adapters or side networks.
- Go beyond two tasks with a projection. Projection experiments use 2 tasks only, and the 11-task analysis tracks only task 1's readout.
- Test cumulative null spaces over k tasks. These are discussed only for deep LINEAR networks (App. A.3), described as expensive (n(k−1) null spaces, recomputed every step) and possibly too small, and left as "needs to be tested empirically".
- Use RL, robotics or closed-loop control.

Corrections to the searcher:
- Exactness is not missing. Their linear case is exact at every input, including off-distribution inputs, and needs no data. Exactness is lost only in the deep nonlinear version.
- TinyImageNet appears only in an appendix, as an EWC/replay drift analysis, not with the null-space method.
verdict.exact_delta:
NSA cannot claim the null-space idea or exact retention as new. Anthes et al. already split the shared last layer into old-head range and null space, already state that null-space change is free, and already give an exact, data-free null-space update for a one-hidden-layer linear network; for one new skill that update is the same as a linear NSA adapter on the raw input (h' = W_H x + NNᵀΔW_H x). What NSA does that they do not:
- Exact, data-free retention in a deep NONLINEAR network at every state, including closed-loop states. NSA gets this by applying the old-head projector to an additive adapter's output on a frozen trunk. Anthes et al. say weight-gradient projection cannot do this, so their deep version uses an approximate projection that needs old-task data.
- A cumulative projector over all previous heads, with later adapters reading earlier adapters' features. Anthes et al. test only 2 tasks and leave k-task null-space intersections untested.
- The random-adapter / copied-head initialization, and RL robot skills.

What they do that NSA does not: keep the whole backbone plastic with no added parameters, and analyse range vs null-space drift for EWC/SI/LwF/replay/GEM over 11 tasks. Their deep method is the direct precedent for a no-added-parameter, gradient-projection baseline such as FN-PPO, if that is how FN-PPO works. Verdict: cite this paper as NSA's closest conceptual precursor. NSA's defensible novelty is the exact deep-network architectural version, the multi-skill chain, and closed-loop RL evidence. For a single new skill, NSA adds little beyond Anthes et al.'s linear projector combined with side-tuning.

papers.title: Progressive Neural Networks
papers.authors: Andrei A. Rusu, Neil C. Rabinowitz, Guillaume Desjardins, Hubert Soyer, James Kirkpatrick, Koray Kavukcuoglu, Razvan Pascanu, Raia Hadsell
papers.venue_year: arXiv 2016 (1606.04671). Robot RL version: Rusu et al., 'Sim-to-Real Robot Learning from Pixels with Progressive Nets', CoRL 2017, PMLR 78:262-270
papers.mechanism: Each new task gets a new column and all earlier columns are frozen. The new column receives lateral connections from the hidden layers of every earlier column; these are small adapter MLPs that reduce dimension. It has its own output head, so earlier tasks cannot be forgotten. Width and lateral parameters grow with every task. The CoRL 2017 paper uses this for sparse-reward, pixel-based sim-to-real arm RL, where the real-robot column reads the frozen sim column.
papers.overlap: Already does: frozen trunk; a new trainable module that reads the input and earlier hidden layers (NSA's adapter reading x and trunk layer 2 is a PNN lateral connection); exact retention at every state with no stored data; later tasks reuse earlier tasks' features. Does not: write back into one shared fixed-width vector. Each column keeps its own layer, so PNN never needs a projector, and its width grows. Reported bars (from other papers): Meta-World, 20 tasks: performance 0.41, forward transfer -0.04 (CompoNet, Table 1). Brax: performance about 1.0 at 4-8x model size (CSP, Table 1).
papers.setting: RL (Atari, Labyrinth; robot sim-to-real RL in CoRL 2017); task-incremental with known task ID

papers.title: Side-Tuning: A Baseline for Network Adaptation via Additive Side Networks
papers.authors: Jeffrey O. Zhang, Alexander Sax, Amir Zamir, Leonidas Guibas, Jitendra Malik
papers.mechanism: A frozen pretrained network is adapted by training a small side network. The side network's output is added to the frozen network's output through a blending weight. In incremental learning with known task IDs, each task gets its own side branch on the unchanged base, and the paper reports no catastrophic forgetting. It also runs RL and imitation (Habitat navigation) experiments.
papers.overlap: Already does: NSA's one-new-skill case, i.e. frozen base, additive side branch, new head, exact retention, no data. This is the baseline a reviewer will call 'the same thing' for PickCube->StackCube. Does not: chains of skills writing into the same shared vector. Each task's sum is private, so no projection is needed.
papers.setting: Supervised incremental learning (iCIFAR, iTaskonomy), plus RL and imitation; task-incremental

papers.title: Self-Composing Policies for Scalable Continual Reinforcement Learning (CompoNet)
papers.authors: Mikel Malagón, Josu Ceberio, Jose A. Lozano
papers.mechanism: A modular policy that grows: for each new task, all earlier modules are frozen and one new module is added. The new module attends over the stacked action outputs of all earlier modules (an output-attention head and an input-attention head) and adds an internal MLP policy that can copy, adjust or override them. Parameters grow linearly with the number of tasks. Retention follows from freezing.
papers.overlap: Already does: continual RL with frozen earlier skills and exact retention by construction. A new skill can copy the best earlier policy (similar to NSA's head-copy init) and reuse earlier skills. Does not: share a fixed-width feature vector. Composition happens at the action-output level, with no null-space projection. Numbers (arXiv 2506.14811 version): Meta-World 20 tasks, 1M SAC steps each: performance 0.42 vs ProgressiveNet 0.41, FT-N 0.37, PackNet 0.24; forward transfer 0.01 vs PNN -0.04. The gap to PNN is within the error bars. ALE SpaceInvaders 0.99/0.74, Freeway 0.94/0.80.
papers.setting: RL (SAC on Meta-World, PPO on ALE); task-incremental

papers.title: Order parameters and phase transitions of continual learning in deep neural networks
papers.authors: Haozhe Shan, Qianyi Li, Haim Sompolinsky
papers.mechanism: A statistical-physics theory of continual learning in deep, wide networks with task-specific readouts and a penalty on weight change. It shows that when the hidden representation changes only within the null space of task 1's readout, task 1's output is unchanged, i.e. zero forgetting. It also maps the phases where this holds and where it breaks. The zero-forgetting phase can coincide with 'catastrophic anterograde interference', where the new task fails to learn.
papers.overlap: Already states NSA's core invariance in writing: in a multi-head network, representation changes in the null space of old readouts leave old outputs exactly intact. Does not: propose an explicit projector, adapters, or anything robotic or RL. In the paper the null-space confinement emerges from an L2 penalty rather than being built in. Its anterograde-interference phase mirrors your GPM-blocking failure.
papers.setting: Supervised theory; multi-head, task-incremental

papers.title: TAIL: Task-specific Adapters for Imitation Learning with Large Pretrained Models
papers.authors: Zuxin Liu, Jesse Zhang, Kavosh Asadi, Yao Liu, Ding Zhao, Shoham Sabach, Rasool Fakoor
papers.mechanism: A large pretrained language-conditioned manipulation policy is kept frozen, and each new task gets its own parameter-efficient adapter. LoRA works best; bottleneck adapters and prompt/prefix tuning are also tested. The adapter is chosen by task, so earlier tasks are never touched.
papers.overlap: Already does: frozen base plus a small additive module per task, giving exact retention (BWT 0) without replay in robot learning. Does not: share features between skills (each task gets its own forward pass with its own LoRA), shared-vector projection, or RL. Numbers: LoRA trains 2.02M params, 1.17% of 172M. LIBERO-10 forward success 0.70 vs full fine-tuning 0.48, ER 0.45, EWC 0.30. Full fine-tuning forgets earlier suites (Spatial 0.79->0.53, Goal 0.42->0.20). Frozen features with only new heads was near zero, consistent with your slow head-only baseline.
papers.setting: Imitation (LIBERO); task-incremental with task ID

papers.title: OrthoSkillVLA: Continual Skill Learning via Gradient-Informed Skill Subspace Adaptation
papers.authors: Jiaqi Wang, Zhou Fang, Qiongfeng Shi, Yi Zhou
papers.mechanism: Replay-free continual skill learning on a pretrained X-VLA (~0.9B). After each skill it stores an orthonormal basis of gradient directions for each adapted layer. For a new skill, LoRA's down-projection A is initialised from the top singular vectors of the gradient with that basis projected out, then frozen, and only B is trained. The VLM and the action head get separate energy thresholds. A tiny per-skill decoder expert (about 0.0046% of the model) is picked by a training-free feature-similarity router.
papers.overlap: Already does: keeps new-skill learning out of old skills' subspace and adds per-skill output experts, in a robot policy; it also notes the action head is where forgetting concentrates. Does not: give exact retention. Protection is first-order, in weight space, and confined only through initialisation (NBT 0.13), i.e. the GPM-like family you found fails in closed loop. Imitation, not RL. Numbers: LIBERO-derived, 3 skills: final success 83.5%/NBT 0.13 vs KeepLoRA 56.6%/0.46, SeqLoRA 32.4%/0.89, O-LoRA 30.5%/0.85. Real robot, 4 skills: 86.25% vs 71.25%.
papers.setting: Imitation (VLA); skill-incremental, router picks the expert; sim + real

papers.title: Continual Learning in Low-rank Orthogonal Subspaces (ORTHOG-SUBSPACE)
papers.authors: Arslan Chaudhry, Naeemullah Khan, Puneet K. Dokania, Philip H. S. Torr
papers.mechanism: Each task gets a fixed random rank-r projection P_t = O_t O_t^T of the shared m-dimensional last hidden layer. The projections are mutually orthogonal across tasks, so the last layer's gradients for different tasks are orthogonal by construction. The whole network is still trained; interference in earlier layers is reduced by keeping weights orthonormal (Stiefel-manifold optimisation) and by a small replay memory.
papers.overlap: Already does: gives each task a budget of disjoint low-dimensional directions in one shared fixed-width feature, with task-specific heads (the analogue of NSA's '8 of 256 dims per skill'). Does not: freeze anything. Retention is approximate because earlier layers still interfere and replay is used. The subspaces are fixed random rather than defined by learned heads, there are no additive adapters, and there is no RL.
papers.setting: Supervised (MNIST/CIFAR/miniImageNet); task-incremental

papers.title: Sparse Diffusion Policy: A Sparse, Reusable, and Flexible Policy for Robot Learning
papers.authors: Yixiao Wang, Yifei Zhang, Mingxiao Huo, Ran Tian, Xiang Zhang, Yichen Xie, Chenfeng Xu, Pengliang Ji, Wei Zhan, Mingyu Ding, Masayoshi Tomizuka
papers.mechanism: A transformer diffusion policy with mixture-of-experts layers and a task-specific router. For continual learning it freezes all earlier experts, routers and non-MoE modules, and each new task adds new experts (8, of which 2 are active) plus a new router. The new router can also select old experts.
papers.overlap: Already does: frozen base plus additive per-task modules, reuse of old experts by new skills, and constant active parameters. Does not: a shared-vector projection or RL. Numbers (robomimic Can->Lift->Square): SDP Can 0.96->0.94, Lift 1.00->1.00, Square 0.75. Full fine-tuning drops Can and Lift to 0.00. LoRA keeps old tasks, but its active params grow from 9.0M to 14.9M, against a constant 9.2M for SDP. The claimed exactness is not quite borne out by its own table (0.96->0.94).
papers.setting: Imitation (diffusion policy); task-incremental via task-specific router

papers.title: Building a Subspace of Policies for Scalable Continual Learning (CSP)
papers.authors: Jean-Baptiste Gaya, Thang Doan, Lucas Caccia, Laure Soulier, Ludovic Denoyer, Roberta Raileanu
papers.mechanism: Keeps a simplex of policies whose vertices (anchors) are full parameter vectors, and stores each learned task as a single vector of convex-combination weights. For a new task it trains one new anchor with the old anchors frozen. It keeps the anchor only if the best policy in the enlarged subspace beats the old subspace by a threshold, so parameters grow sublinearly.
papers.overlap: Already does: exact retention without replay (frozen anchors plus a stored weight vector reproduce each old policy exactly), reuse of old solutions, and RL on locomotion and manipulation. Does not: share a fixed-width feature vector or use heads in its main variant. Numbers: CW10 performance 0.81 vs PackNet 0.83, EWC 0.66, FT-1 0.10, using about 5.3 heads instead of 10. Brax HalfCheetah 1.27 at 5.4x model size vs PNN 1.03 at 8x.
papers.setting: RL (SAC; Brax, Continual World); task-incremental

papers.title: Incremental Learning of Retrievable Skills For Efficient Continual Task Adaptation (IsCiL)
papers.authors: Daehee Lee, Minjong Yoo, Woo Kyung Kim, Wonje Choi, Honguk Woo
papers.mechanism: A fixed pretrained diffusion policy is modulated by per-skill LoRA adapters (rank 4, about 1.5% of parameters each). A prototype memory in a state-embedding space retrieves the adapter to use at each state. A new adapter starts as a copy of the existing adapter with the highest retrieval score and is trained on the new demonstrations without rehearsal.
papers.overlap: Already does: frozen base plus per-skill additive adapters, with each new skill initialised from the closest old skill (like NSA's head copy). Does not: claim exact retention (BWT is non-zero, even positive, because skills are shared); no shared-vector projection; imitation, not RL. Numbers: Franka-Kitchen-Complete FWT/BWT/AUC 79.3/11.0/89.8 vs TAIL-τ 86.2/0.0/86.2 and Seq-FT 90.9/-63.7/35.0. With incomplete demos, AUC 74.0 vs TAIL-τ 33.8.
papers.setting: Imitation (Franka-Kitchen, Meta-World); skill retrieval without task ID

papers.title: Lifelong Language-Conditioned Robotic Manipulation Learning (SkillsCrafter)
papers.authors: Xudong Wang, Zebin Han, Zhiyu Liu, Gan Li, Jiahua Dong, Baichen Liu, Lianqing Liu, Zhi Han
papers.mechanism: LoRA on a pretrained LLARVA manipulation agent. The A factor is skill-shared and is initialised by a similarity-weighted aggregation of earlier skills' A. The B factor is skill-specific, with a soft orthogonality penalty against earlier skills' B (λ=0.1). A Gumbel-softmax gate decides per layer whether to inject LoRA, and SVD over instruction embeddings aggregates skills at inference time.
papers.overlap: Already does: orthogonality between skills' adapters to limit interference, initialisation from similar old skills, and real-robot skills. Does not: give exact retention (the penalty is soft, forgetting rate 16.0%), use feature null-space, or RL. Numbers: 18 skills (12 sim, 6 real): 52.0% average success / 16.0% forgetting vs SD-LoRA+SkSA 50.0%/20.8% and O-LoRA+SkSA 49.1%.
papers.setting: Imitation (LLM-based manipulation agent); skill-incremental; sim + real

papers.title: ACCRUE: Continual Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Robot Foundation Models
papers.authors: Changyeon Kim, Kimin Lee, Yashraj Narang, Yijie Guo
papers.mechanism: Continual off-policy RL on top of a robot foundation model (GR00T N1.7 in sim, π0.5 on hardware). The base is fine-tuned on demos and held fixed during each stage's RL. A lightweight actor, which refines the base's action chunk from frozen DINOv3 features, proprioception and the base chunk, and a distributional critic are carried from stage to stage. Earlier tasks are retained by distilling the actor toward a frozen copy of the previous actor on the last 50-200 retained episodes per task, mixed 1:1 with current data.
papers.overlap: Already does: a residual RL module on a frozen base, reuse of earlier actor and critic for forward transfer, and contact-rich insertion in sim and on a real robot. This sets the current sample-efficiency bar for robot RL. Does not: give exact retention (it uses distillation, final forgetting about 0.05-0.07); there is one shared actor with no per-skill head, and it needs stored episodes. Numbers: FORGE, 3 tasks, 500K steps per stage: NBT 0.065, forgetting 0.068, final 0.917. AutoMate 5-stage: NBT 0.047. Real robot: 31.0-68.5% less RL time to 95% success than single-task RL, 19.4/20 retention.
papers.setting: Off-policy RL on VLA / robot foundation model; sim + real; task given by language instruction

papers.title: Simple Recipe Works: Vision-Language-Action Models are Natural Continual Learners with Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Jiaheng Hu, Jay Shim, Chen Tang, Yoonchang Sung, Bo Liu, Peter Stone, Roberto Martín-Martín
papers.mechanism: A systematic study of continual RL for VLAs: OpenVLA-OFT (also π0 and OpenVLA) trained with on-policy GRPO on LIBERO, RoboCasa and ManiSkill. Plain sequential fine-tuning with rank-32 LoRA is compared with EWC, replay, a parameter-isolation baseline (DWE), SLCA, RETAIN and others. The authors attribute the low forgetting to large pretraining, LoRA and on-policy RL together.
papers.overlap: Not an NSA-like method, but the main threat and bar. Sequential LoRA RL fine-tuning reaches NBT 0.3 / 1.0 / -2.4 on LIBERO Spatial/Object/Long with positive forward transfer. The isolation baseline (DWE) gets NBT 0.0 but slightly lower success (79.6 vs 81.2 on Spatial) and zero forward transfer. It also supports your regime: their small 12M policy forgets (NBT 11.4) and full fine-tuning forgets (NBT 40.9).
papers.setting: On-policy RL (GRPO) on VLAs; task-incremental with language

papers.title: Fine-tuning Reinforcement Learning Models is Secretly a Forgetting Mitigation Problem
papers.authors: Maciej Wołczyk, Bartłomiej Cupiał, Mateusz Ostaszewski, Michał Bortkiewicz, Michał Zając, Razvan Pascanu, Łukasz Kuciński, Piotr Miłoś
papers.mechanism: Shows that RL fine-tuning of a pretrained policy destroys competence in 'far' states, which are reached only later in an episode, because early fine-tuning visits only 'close' states. Knowledge-retention terms fix it: behavioral cloning on stored data, kickstarting/KL, EWC, episodic memory. On RoboticSequence (4 chained Meta-World stages) BC worked best; on NetHack kickstarting worked best (score from about 5K to over 10K).
papers.overlap: Proposes no architecture. It gives the closed-loop forgetting diagnosis that matches your finding (forgetting concentrates after the grasp and compounds), and it supplies the BC/KL distillation baselines that NSA has to beat on data-free retention.
papers.setting: RL fine-tuning (NetHack, Montezuma's Revenge, Meta-World RoboticSequence)

papers.title: Memory Anchors for Continual Robot Learning
papers.authors: Maximilian Du, Zhanyi Sun, Chen Xu, Paarth Shah, Masha Itkina, Shuran Song
papers.mechanism: Replay-based continual imitation. It finds 'memory anchors': old-task samples nearest to new-task samples whose latent representations overlap old data but whose actions conflict with the old policy. It then over-weights these anchors in the replay buffer (AnchorER).
papers.overlap: Background. It frames forgetting as representation overlap plus action conflict, the same situation as your finding that StackCube lives inside PickCube's subspace. It needs stored data and gives neither architectural isolation nor exact retention. Numbers: removing 10% of anchors gives more than 4.5x the forgetting; adding anchors cuts forgetting on high-conflict pairs by 63%; LIBERO-Goal NBT 0.18->0.11; π0.5 forgetting down 22%; real-robot final success 1.7x that of random replay.
papers.setting: Imitation (diffusion policy; π0.5 VLA); sim + real; task-incremental with replay

searches.notes:
VERDICT: I did not find the same idea. I searched robot continual RL and imitation learning (2016 to Oct 2026), continual LoRA for VLAs, and the null-space / orthogonal continual-learning literature. No paper adds a skill by projecting an adapter's additive feature write onto the null space of all earlier linear policy heads inside one shared, fixed-width layer to get exact retention.
- Null-space / orthogonal methods: GPM, Adam-NSCL, InfLoRA, NSP², NuSA-CL, OrthoSkillVLA, SkillsCrafter and the LLM preprint Brainstacks all constrain weights or gradients against input or feature subspaces. They are approximate and protect only the data seen so far, not every state.
- Isolation methods: PNN, side-tuning, CompoNet, CSP, PackNet, TAIL, SDP and IsCiL keep old tasks by freezing or isolating them. None writes into a shared stream.
- Residual policies on a frozen base: ACCRUE uses distillation; FAST ([arXiv 2602.11929](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11929)) uses soft Parseval and KL constraints. Neither gives exact retention.

DO NOT OVERSELL:
1. The invariance itself is elementary and already in print. Shan, Li & Sompolinsky (PNAS 2026) state that in a multi-head network, representation changes inside the null space of an old readout leave that task's outputs unchanged. Neuroscience calls the same thing "output-null" activity ([Kaufman et al., Nature Neuroscience 2014](https://doi.org/10.1038/nn.3643)). Robotics reviewers know null-space projection from task-priority control. Expect "the projector is one line of linear algebra".
2. Exact retention at every closed-loop state with no stored data is NOT new. PNN, side-tuning, CompoNet, CSP, PackNet, per-task LoRA (TAIL) and SDP all get it by freezing. It only separates NSA from three other families: weight-space projection (which you found fails in closed loop), distillation (ACCRUE; Wołczyk et al.'s BC/KL) and replay (Memory Anchors, LOTUS, M2Distill).
3. For one new skill, NSA is a progressive column or side network whose head also reads the old features. Concatenating [h; g] with an unprojected adapter also keeps Pick exact.

The defensible contribution is therefore an architectural variant: a fixed-width progressive network in which every column writes into one shared stream through a head-null-space projector. That buys:
- one forward pass for all skills;
- a fixed head input width;
- a clear capacity budget of 256/8 = 32 skills (fewer if critics or other per-skill readouts also read h, since they must be inside P too);
- automatic reuse of earlier adapters' features by later skills.
The random-not-zero initialisation point is real but small; it is related to known function-preserving-growth issues (e.g. GradMax).

IMPLICATIONS FOR THE RSS ABSTRACT:
- The k=2 PickCube->StackCube result shows nothing that isolation methods cannot.
- Expected baselines: a PNN column; side-tuning, i.e. an unprojected adapter with a head reading [h; g]; CompoNet; per-skill LoRA on the trunk; PackNet; ideally CSP. Run them on a chain of 3 or more skills, where the shared stream should pay off (forward transfer to skill 3, steps to 90%, parameters).
- Parameter bar: TAIL 1.17% per task; IsCiL about 1.5% (rank-4 LoRA); OrthoSkillVLA about 0.005% per skill expert; SDP constant active parameters; CSP sublinear (about 5 anchors/heads for 8-10 tasks). At +25-100% of the trunk per skill, NSA looks heavy unless you report absolute counts (the trunk is tiny) and show the extra parameters buy speed.
- Speed bar: CompoNet uses 1M SAC steps per Meta-World task at PNN-level performance. ACCRUE cuts real-robot RL time by 31-68.5% versus single-task RL, with about 0.05-0.07 forgetting. No paper reports steps-to-90% on ManiSkill Pick->Stack, so your numbers have no direct comparison.
- Threat: Hu et al. (RLC 2026) and Liu et al. ([arXiv 2603.03818](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03818)) report that large pretrained VLAs forget little with LoRA or small replay. Hu et al. also show a small 12M policy (NBT 11.4) and full fine-tuning (NBT 40.9) do forget. That supports your small-policy setting, but the paper must argue why exact retention matters (long skill chains, safety) or demonstrate NSA on a VLA action head.

CONFIRMED BUT NOT LISTED:
- [OWL, Kessler et al., AAAI 2022](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/20674): shared trunk + per-task heads + EWC + bandit. This is NSA's base architecture without exact retention.
- [Progress & Compress, Schwarz et al., ICML 2018](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/schwarz18a.html): active column distilled into an EWC-protected knowledge base; approximate retention.
- [LOTUS, Wan et al., ICRA 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.02058): skill library + replay.
- [M2Distill, Roy et al., ICRA 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.00064): multi-modal distillation.
- [PackNet, Mallya & Lazebnik, CVPR 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.05769): 0.83 on CW10, the best score in CSP's table.

verdict.what_it_does:
I checked this against the full text of both PDFs.

**PNN (2016), Section 2, Eqs. 1-2.** Column 1 is trained to convergence. For each new task k, the parameters of all earlier columns are frozen and a new column is created with its own full stack of layers and random initialisation. Layer i of the new column computes h_i^(k) = f(W_i^(k) h_{i-1}^(k) + sum_{j<k} U_i^(k:j) h_{i-1}^(j)). So each layer of the new column reads the layer below it in every earlier column, all the way up to the output layer. The policy is the top layer of the column, and each column has its own A3C policy and value outputs.

In practice each lateral link is an "adapter": a one-hidden-layer MLP over the concatenated features of the earlier columns. Its input is scaled by a learned scalar alpha and reduced by a learned matrix V (a 1x1 conv for conv layers), which keeps the lateral parameter count on the order of one column. Note that this "projection onto an n_i-dimensional subspace" is a learned down-projection. It is not an orthogonal or null-space projector.

Lateral links run only from old columns to new ones. Old columns are therefore unaffected in the forward pass and, being frozen, are kept exactly at every state with no stored data (the paper calls them "immune to forgetting"). The task label is needed at test time. Units grow linearly with the number of tasks and parameters grow quadratically (Appendix B). Experiments use A3C on Pong variants, Atari and Labyrinth. Transfer is measured as area under the learning curve relative to one column trained from scratch.

**CoRL 2017 robot version.** The simulation column is wide and the real-robot columns are narrow: 37-39K parameters (including laterals) versus 299-621K, about 6-12%. Laterals feed every conv and LSTM layer, and no adapters are used on the output layer.

The new column is initialised so that its first policy is identical to the old one. The new head's weights reading the old column's last layer are copied from the old head. Its weights reading the new column's own last layer start at zero, and everything else starts random.

The task is a Jaco arm learning from RGB pixels with a sparse +1 reward for reaching the target. The progressive column reached 34 points in about 60k real-robot steps. The from-scratch columns got zero reward, and fine-tuning finished below the progressive column. A three-column chain (reach in simulation, then reach on the real robot with proprioception, then track a target moving on a pulley) transferred almost immediately.

**The searcher's figures from other papers are correct.**
- CompoNet (ICML 2024, arXiv 2506.14811), Table 1, Meta-World CW20 (10 tasks repeated twice, 1M steps per task, 10 seeds): ProgNet performance 0.41 +/- 0.49 and forward transfer -0.04 +/- 0.04. CompoNet itself scores 0.42 and 0.01.
- CSP (ICLR 2023, arXiv 2211.10445), Table 1, with performance normalised so that one SAC policy per task scores 1.00: PNN scores 1.03 / 0.98 / 0.98 on HalfCheetah / Ant / Humanoid at 8.0x / 8.0x / 4.0x model size. CSP cut PNN's layer count so its size stays capped.
verdict.exact_delta: The one thing NSA adds that PNN lacks is the direction of writing: NSA adds each new module's output into one fixed-width 256-d vector that every head reads, projected onto the null space of all earlier heads' rows (I - P_<k), whereas PNN adds old features into each new column's own vector (old to new only), so it never needs a projector. The cost is that NSA keeps a constant per-skill size but has a cap of about 32 skills, while PNN grows linearly in units and quadratically in lateral links. PNN has what NSA lacks: a full new layer stack per task with laterals into every layer, new input types such as proprioception, and real-robot results including a three-task chain. Everything in NSA's single-skill Pick-to-Stack result is already in PNN and its CoRL 2017 robot version, including the new head copied from the old head with zero weight on the new features and a random new module (NSA's "random, not zero" subtlety). Because task IDs are known and adapters read only the input and frozen trunk layers, a chain without projection (head j reads h0 plus the sum of g_i for i up to j) would also keep old skills exactly, so the paper must show what the shared null-space vector buys over a narrow-column PNN at k >= 3, with PNN as a required baseline.

verdict.correct_citation: Jeffrey O. Zhang, Alexander Sax, Amir Zamir, Leonidas Guibas, Jitendra Malik. "Side-Tuning: A Baseline for Network Adaptation via Additive Side Networks." Computer Vision - ECCV 2020 (Spotlight), Springer LNCS 12348, pp. 698-714, 2020. DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-58580-8_41. Also arXiv:1912.13503 (v1 31 Dec 2019; v4 31 Jul 2020). Checked against the arXiv abstract page, the full PDF text, Crossref (pages 698-714, published online 3 Dec 2020) and the ECVA listing. The ECVA file is named 123480698.pdf, which points to LNCS volume 12348, starting page 698. The searcher's title, authors, venue, DOI and link are all correct.
verdict.what_it_does: The base model B(x) is frozen and has no learnable parameters. It can be a pretrained net, a decision tree or an oracle. A side network S(x) reads only the raw input and is fused with the base output late: R(x) = alpha*B(x) + (1-alpha)*S(x). alpha is learned or follows a schedule: alpha=1 is feature extraction, and alpha=0 with S copied from B is fine-tuning. The paper also compares product, MLP (as in progressive networks) and FiLM merges, which perform about the same. S starts as a copy of the base, or is distilled from it when the architectures differ; a "low-energy" start trained not to change the output and Xavier init are also tested. For incremental learning with known task IDs (iCIFAR: 10 tasks, ResNet-44 base pretrained on CIFAR-10; iTaskonomy: 12 tasks, ResNet-50 base), each task t gets its own side network S_t, blend weight alpha_t and decoder D_t. These are trained with loss ||D_t(alpha_t*B(x) + (1-alpha_t)*S_t(x)) - y_t|| and then frozen. Earlier tasks therefore cannot be forgotten, with no stored data and no regularizer, and later tasks do not learn more slowly. It ranks first on iTaskonomy against EWC, PSP, PNN, Piggyback and residual adapters, and second on iCIFAR, behind PNN. RL and imitation appear only as two-task transfer: a visual encoder pretrained on a Taskonomy task (curvature or denoising) is side-tuned for Habitat point-goal navigation, by behaviour cloning or by PPO for 10M frames. No earlier control skill is kept or evaluated for retention. The other domains are SQuAD v2 with BERT and Taskonomy transfer. Side networks are never shared or chained across tasks; the paper lists reusing them as future work ("Leveraging previously trained side networks could yield better performance on later tasks"). Its only experiment with several side networks is boosting many side networks for a single task, which did worse than one deeper network.
verdict.exact_delta: What NSA does that side-tuning does not: every skill's adapter writes into one shared 256-d vector that all heads read, and the adapter output is projected away from the row space of all earlier heads, so later heads can read features from earlier adapters while every earlier head's output stays exactly the same. NSA's adapter also reads the trunk's second hidden layer, whereas side-tuning fuses late and S reads only the input. NSA warm-starts the new head as a copy of the closest old head, and it tests retention in closed loop on robot skills; side-tuning has no projection, no shared vector across tasks, and its only RL is vision-to-navigation transfer that keeps no old skill. What side-tuning does that NSA does not: a learnable alpha blend that rescales the base features, black-box bases, side networks copied or distilled from the base, other merge operators, and 10-task and 12-task supervised incremental benchmarks. For a single new skill (PickCube->StackCube), NSA is an instance of side-tuning: frozen base, additive side branch, new head, exact retention without data or a regularizer, known task IDs, and even PPO. That result is not novel on its own. A caveat on the delta: the heads are linear and frozen, so under NSA each head j outputs exactly what it would get from its own prefix sum h_j (level(k) in /home/ryan/Documents/pve/wrwl/nsa.py already computes this). A chain without projection, where head j reads h_0+g_1+...+g_j, gives the same exact retention and the same reuse of earlier adapters, without spending 8 dimensions per skill. The projection therefore only buys the single shared vector and the exact warm start from a copied head, which a zero-initialised extra head block would also give. Reviewers will likely ask you to justify it.

verdict.correct_citation: Mikel Malagón, Josu Ceberio, Jose A. Lozano. "Self-Composing Policies for Scalable Continual Reinforcement Learning." Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2024, oral), PMLR 235:34432-34460, 2024. arXiv:2506.14811 (v1, posted June 2025). OpenReview: f5gtX2VWSB. verdict.what_it_does:
Checked against the PMLR page and the arXiv HTML (Sec. 2 and 4, Table 1, Appendices A, C and E).

How it grows: CompoNet adds one module per task and freezes every earlier module.

What a module reads: for a given state, module k gets two inputs:
- h_s, which is the raw state for low-dimensional tasks ("h_s = s"). For images, h_s comes from the module's own CNN encoder, initialised from the previous module's encoder.
- Phi, a (k-1) x |A| matrix holding the action outputs of all earlier modules (Gaussian means, or action probabilities).

How a module computes its output:
- Output-attention head (query from h_s, keys from Phi plus a positional code, values = Phi itself) produces a tentative action v. It is a softmax-weighted mix of the earlier policies' outputs.
- Input-attention head summarises [v; Phi].
- An internal MLP policy with its own hidden layers reads that summary and h_s. It outputs an |A|-vector that is added to v, which the paper calls "akin to residual connections".
- So a module can copy one earlier policy (attention picks it, the MLP outputs zero), combine several, or ignore them and learn from scratch.

Retention: earlier modules are frozen, and module i depends only on modules before it, so its outputs stay exactly the same. The paper reports forgetting only for Baseline and FT-1. It assumes task boundaries and task IDs are known.

Communication between modules: only action-space vectors pass between modules. The paper says it composes policies "instead of sharing hidden layer representations" and sets this against ProgressiveNet's lateral connections.

Cost: parameters grow linearly, one full module per task. Inference is quadratic in the number of tasks in theory, though they measured sub-quadratic growth up to 300 tasks.

Related work: Section 2 does not mention null space, orthogonal projection, adapters, side-tuning, GPM or OWL.

Results (Table 1, 10 seeds):
- Meta-World, 20 tasks (10 tasks seen twice), SAC, 1M steps per task. Performance: CompoNet 0.42+-0.49, ProgressiveNet 0.41+-0.49, FT-N 0.37+-0.48, PackNet 0.24+-0.40, Baseline 0.06. Forward transfer: CompoNet 0.01+-0.14, ProgressiveNet -0.04+-0.04.
- ALE SpaceInvaders (performance / forward transfer): CompoNet 0.99/0.74, FT-N 0.99/0.73.
- ALE Freeway (performance / forward transfer): CompoNet 0.94/0.80, FT-N 0.81/0.64.

The searcher described the mechanism and the numbers accurately. Its "very close" rating is too strong for the mechanism. Also, "can copy the best earlier policy" is a learned, state-dependent attention choice, not a copy made at initialisation.
verdict.exact_delta:
What NSA does that CompoNet does not: NSA keeps one shared 256-d vector that every head reads, and each new skill writes new features into it through a small adapter (+6-100% of the trunk), projected into the null space of all earlier heads. Later skills can therefore reuse hidden features written by earlier adapters, with O(n) inference and no attention. CompoNet passes only |A|-dimensional action outputs between modules (explicitly "instead of sharing hidden layer representations"), each module learns its own features from the raw state, and its "copy an old policy" is a learned attention choice, not NSA's copy-the-closest-head initialisation.

What CompoNet does that NSA does not: it can grow without limit, whereas NSA's 256-d width caps it at about 32 skills of 8 directions each. It can select and override among all earlier policies depending on the state. And it has 20-task Meta-World and ALE results with public code.

Both keep old skills exactly by construction (frozen, cascaded modules plus known task IDs), so neither exact retention nor policy reuse is new for NSA. NSA's claim has to rest on the shared null-space feature stream, shown in chains of k >= 3 skills against CompoNet and ProgressiveNet. CompoNet's own gap over ProgressiveNet was within the error bars (0.42 vs 0.41, +-0.49).

synthesis.verdict_text: Incremental. Four searches found no paper with NSA's exact construction: per-skill residual adapters on a frozen deep policy, whose post-nonlinearity writes are projected onto the joint null space of all earlier linear heads, inside one fixed-width vector that every head reads, tested with PPO in closed loop. So it is not literally done already. One unconfirmed lead should still be read before submission: CNSP, an ICLR 2026 OpenReview submission whose abstract names 'head preservation'. Everything the Pick→Stack result shows is already published, though. Exact, data-free retention by freezing and adding modules, with reuse of old features and even the same copied-head/random-new-module start, is in Progressive Nets (including the CoRL 2017 robot version), Side-Tuning, Ternary Feature Masks and CompoNet. The output-side rule, that writes in the null space of all earlier heads leave them exactly unchanged, is in Peng & Risteski (NeurIPS 2022, for a shared fixed-width linear feature vector) and Anthes et al. (CoLLAs 2024). With known skill IDs and linear heads, NSA is concatenation-style growth with tied weights. An unprojected variant, in which head j reads its own prefix h0+g1+…+gj, is bitwise exact, reuses every earlier adapter and spends no dimensions. So for now the projection is a cost, not a demonstrated contribution. What is still open is empirical. Does the write-protected shared stream learn new skills faster than prefix-sum, concatenation, PNN, per-skill LoRA, PackNet and CompoNet in 4–5-skill chains and on an a2r Isaac Lab pair, or do better at fixed width? Alongside that sits the closed-loop evidence that approximate protection fails after the grasp. If the projection ablation ties, the honest paper is a fixed-width progressive network for robot skill addition plus a closed-loop forgetting analysis: workshop strength, not a main-track method.

closest.citation: Binghui Peng, Andrej Risteski. 'Continual learning: a feature extraction formalization, an efficient algorithm, and fundamental obstructions.' NeurIPS 2022 (NeurIPS 35, pp. 28414-28427); arXiv 2203.14383. Verified. The camera-ready PDF header ends '...and barriers'; its experiments appear only in the camera-ready and supplement.
closest.what_it_does: Theory of task-incremental, multi-head learning with a fixed-width shared linear representation R(x)=U^T x and one frozen linear head per environment. DPGrad projects every update of U as P_W-perp grad_U P_V-perp, where V spans all earlier heads. Each earlier head's predictions therefore stay exactly fixed at every input with no stored data, while the new head reads old and new features. New feature directions start as random noise inside the protected complement. The paper proves convergence and no-forgetting bounds. It also proves that a fixed-size learner with nonlinear features cannot avoid forgetting; growing learners are explicitly left open. Experiments: a 500-task synthetic linear chain and 10-task Rotated/Permuted MNIST, where the heuristic ReLU variant DPGrad+ forgets slightly.
closest.what_nsa_adds: NSA adds growth: a frozen nonlinear trunk plus per-skill nonlinear adapters whose post-nonlinearity writes are projected onto the same joint null space. This makes the rule exact for deep policies; their nonlinear variant projects gradients of one shared layer and forgets. NSA also drops their input-side projection (the GPM-like half), copies the closest old head instead of starting a random one, and runs PPO in closed loop. Not new: the null space of all earlier heads inside one shared fixed-width vector, chained heads reading old plus new features, and random seeding of the new directions. Cite it as the linear-case origin and frame NSA as the growth-based escape from its impossibility theorem. NSA has no theory to match it.
